Description: E-text of the *Bhogakārikā* from the *Ratnatraya*, comprising the *Bhogakārikā*, *Nādakārikā*, *Mokṣakārikā*, and *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*, in the Devakottai Series.

Publication year: 1925 Publication city: Devakottai Publication country: India

Having prostrated before Śiva, the bestower of true enjoyment and liberation upon those of dull intellect, [this work] composed by the teacher Sadyojyotiḥśiva, together with the commentary (vṛtti) written by the teacher Aghoraśiva, [is now presented].
For the benefit [of others], I shall provide a clear and brief commentary on the *Bhogakārikā*.

For here, the venerable Sadyojyotiḥpāda, indicating the subject matter consisting of enjoyment and liberation which is to be expounded in this treatise, first performs a salutation to Paramaśiva for the sake of its completion without obstacles.

Having prostrated before the unborn, eternal Śiva, who bestows liberation through the severance of the enjoyment resulting from the union with the power of the mental fluctuations of the three bonds, and who knows the meaning of the sequence of all times; || 1 ||
The "three bonds" (*tribandha*) are those characterized by impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā*; those who possess these are the "three-bound ones" (*tribandhin*).

For these "three-bound ones," known as the *sakalas*, there is this "conjunction with *kalā*"—that is, the connection of their consciousnesses with the constituents of *māyā* consisting of the principles from *kalā* down to earth, which constitute the subtle body and take the form of various worlds and physical bodies.

He who bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*) through that connection and liberation (*mokṣa*) through its disjunction—such is He. By this, Śiva’s state of being eternally liberated (*anādimukta*), His quality of being the benefactor of all, and His status as the creator of all are indicated. For this very reason: "He who knows the meaning of the sequence of all time. This refers to the entire sequence of time consisting of past and so forth, and all...

"He knows the objects existing at each respective time. By this, his omniscience at all times is established, owing to his stainlessness and his status as the creator of all. Furthermore, he is "unborn" (aja), because precisely due to his stainlessness, he is devoid of birth even in the form of a connection with a body and so forth; and he is "constant" (dhruva), meaning changeless, unlike the *bindu* and other such [limited] states.

The state of being subject to transformation [is impossible], because if there were modification, it would entail the consequence of insentience. The connection with what is to be said later is: "Having prostrated to Śiva, I shall speak of enjoyment and liberation. (1)
In order to establish the Ruru-siddhānta, I shall briefly state, refined by reasoning, both enjoyment and liberation along with their means for the sake of the practitioner's understanding.

Those who accomplish both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) are the practitioners (*sādhaka*), such as the teachers (*ācārya*) and others; for their sake, at the beginning of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, the means of accomplishing those [ends] were explained through reasoning (*yukti*) and inference (*anumāna*) in the purified state.
Thus, in the Siddhānta scripture characterized by the venerable *Rauravatantra*, enjoyment and liberation are established along with their respective means.
I shall speak in brief, following the Raurava [Tantra] itself. || 2 ||

In this regard, in order to demonstrate that enjoyment exists for those who possess the means [for it], he states which ones have the capacity for enjoyment: "For those endowed with consciousness, who are impelled by the Lord through the application of ointment and other means, a longing for enjoyment arises in the circle of existence (bhava-maṇḍala) in accordance with their latent impressions of karma. (3)
For those souls who have been impelled by Śiva— the Lord who exists in the state of *adhikāra*— through Ananta and others,

and who are thus turned toward worldly enjoyment, there arises within the sphere of *saṃsāra* a craving for experience (*bhoga-lolika*) according to the ripening of the impressions of their past actions (*karma-saṃskāra*), solely due to the cause of their impurity (*añjana-mala*).

The desire for enjoyment arises. [Objection: But surely the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the Self is inherently pure; [Response: That is incorrect, because attachment to enjoyment is impossible for one who is pure, or else it would follow that even a liberated being could have such attachment. [Objection: But attachment is held to be based on passion (*rāga*); [Response: True, yet even passion is a cause of attachment only for one who is impure. As it has been said:
In the venerable Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa] it is said: "If there is no impurity in the person, how was attachment to enjoyments produced? (3)

Now, what is this enjoyment (bhoga), and by what means is it accomplished? To this he says: "Enjoyment, which consists in the coloring of the modifications of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), is accomplished by means that have fallen away from the seed of the world permeated by the will of God. (4)
The Lord here is indeed Ananta, for he alone is the agitator of Māyā. As it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇatantra:

"In the pure path, Śiva is said to be the agent; in the impure, the Lord Ananta" (Vi. 3.27). From that seed of the universe called Māyā, which has been agitated by His will, there arise non-supporting [entities] consisting of subtle bodies.

The experience that is produced by means such as common and uncommon worlds, as well as by common and uncommon bodies and selves, consists in the coloring of the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). That very thing which is the coloring of the self’s consciousness (*ātma-caitanya*) by the modification of the intellect— characterized by the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of pleasure, pain, and delusion— is indeed experience (*bhoga*).

And here, passion (*anurāga*) consists precisely in the cognition and experience of that [object], by virtue of being established in a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) whose form is the determination of pleasure; it is not, however, the self’s becoming a reflection, for that would entail the consequence of the self undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitā*). As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "The experience of this person is enjoyment, characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth. (4)
In that regard, he first establishes the fact that the elements serve as the means for experience:
"The earth, water, fire, air, and ether—having their respective qualities, functions, and senses nourished by the fullness of their own constituent measures—render [the body] subservient to them. (5)

In this context, those very qualities and so forth belonging to the elements such as earth establish their status as being auxiliary to experience (*bhoga*). Among these, the "qualities" (*guṇa*) are smell and the rest; the "functions" (*vṛtti*), however, are supporting and so forth; and "being the locus of the senses" (*akṣabhūmitā*) means serving as the substratum for the sense organs. He will demonstrate all of these immediately hereafter. And thus, [the elements] beginning with earth...

The meaning is that the elements (bhūtas) serve as the instruments of experience for the selves by means of their qualities (guṇas), their functions (vṛttis), and by being the substratum of the senses. To the question "Of what kind of earth and other elements?", he says: "of those nourished by the filling of their own respective subtle essences" (svamātrāpūrapuṣṭānām). This means: they are nourished by the filling—the act of being filled—by their own respective subtle essences (tanmātras) which serve as their causes. Making what has not been made and increasing what has been made is the function of primordial nature (prakṛti).

And these elements, together with their own causes—the subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—exist as the substrata of the sense organs in both gross and subtle forms; thus it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The subtle elements here [are like] the great elements, which are like jars, while [the senses] are like a coating" (Vi.
19.21). Also in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "This effect, having entered through the instruments, is made to perform activity in ten ways; because of its lack of omnipresence..."

"But the instruments act by presiding over their effects" (Śloka 5). Therefore, while these elements residing in the subtle body share the common nature of being the substratum of the senses— and while those residing in the external body share the nature of being characterized by accumulation (*upacaya*) according to the root-meaning of *dih* (to accumulate) in the sense of "body" (*deha*)— their specific functions are maintenance (*dhṛti*) and so forth.
Thus he says:

"In the earth and the other elements, their functions consist of being instruments, supports, and bodies, as well as sustaining, cohesion, digestion, structural arrangement, and the providing of space. (6)

In that regard, support and maintenance are the function of the earth; cohesion and stability are those of water; cooking and ripening are those of fire; expansion and the joining of parts are those of air; and the granting of space and locus are those of ether.

Now, he describes that very same commonality of theirs as being the substratum of the senses by virtue of residing in the subtle body: "The instrument (karaṇa) residing in the transportive body (ātivāhika-deha), through its expanded [powers], goes from womb to another womb for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyments of the person. (7)

Because it carries the self across [to another state] by means of its own action through the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), destroying that action through experience, it is called the "conveying" (ātivāhika) subtle body; the group of organs, as instruments, functions only while residing therein, for activity is impossible without a support due to their lack of omnipresence.

It has been stated that the group of instruments (the organs) functions only by being supported by the subtle elements residing within the subtle body. Furthermore, that instrument situated in the subtle body, under the influence of karma that brings about the goals of the person, migrates from one womb to another for the sake of accomplishing the experience of that very individual. As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "The collection of principles beginning with the earth is determined for each individual."
"This is the end of time; and by the power of karma, this [time] exists within all the worlds and bodies. (Śloka 24–25). Thus [ends the seventh section].
And that subtle body, because of its subtlety, is not perceptible to people like us—such as Piśācas and others—but is instead accessible through the perception of yogis; thus he says:
"The body is certainly not the *ativāhika*."
This [self], which is supported by the senses and perceivable through them, belongs to those who lack mastery, like a piśāca.

Now he states the qualities of the elements: Odor exists in earth; taste is sixfold, beginning with sweet, in earth and water; white and other colors, as well as bright white, are the quality of form (rūpa) in the three elements beginning with earth.
In earth and air, cold and heat exist separately, as those produced by cooking and those not produced by cooking;
in water, cold touch is established, while in fire, this hot touch is firmly established.
Sound is produced from those substances within the four distinct elements;
it is taught by the wise that the collection of echoes arises only in space.
In that regard, odor—consisting of both fragrant and foul—is found only in earth; taste is found in earth and water.

Among these, in earth it takes the form of pungent, sour, salty, sweet, astringent, and bitter; in water, however, it is exclusively sweet. Color is found in earth, water, and fire. Therein, in earth it is of many kinds, such as white, red, yellow, black, and so forth; in water, however, it is exclusively white; in fire, it is radiant.
In those [elements] together with air, touch resides. And that [touch] in earth and in air is respectively neither cold nor hot.
What, then, is the mutual distinction between the touch of earth and the touch of air? To this he says: "The produced-by-cooking and the not-produced-by-cooking are distinct.

The touch in earth is produced-by-cooking (*pākaja*), whereas in air it is not produced-by-cooking; this alone is the distinction between these two. And because this is an indicative illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*)...
Color and the other qualities of earth are also produced by heating (*pākaja*). In water, however, touch is naturally cold;

in fire, it is hot. Sound, moreover, arises in the four elements beginning with earth through their mutual impact with various substances such as those of an earthly nature. In space (*nabhas*), however, sound consists of echoes.

Now, it might be argued that the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that sound is a unique quality of space (*ākāśa*) because it is not perceived elsewhere than in its substratum; however, this is incorrect. This is because the reason [adduced by them] is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), as it is contradicted by both direct perception and scripture. For sound is heard precisely where its substratum—the drum and so forth—is located. Furthermore, sounds such as the crackling of firewood are observed in earth, and [sounds are likewise observed] in water.
[Sound] consists of *chalacchala* and so forth in fire, *dhamadhamā* and so forth in fire, *śakaśaka* and so forth in air, and in the ether (*nabhas*), it consists of echoes.
Furthermore, this view that sound is a unique quality of space alone has been refuted by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*.
And it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Thus, this sound [exists] in the five [elements], and touch in the four elements; [touch] which is neither cold nor hot..."

Cold and heat belong to earth and wind respectively; [darkness] to water and fire; light belongs to fire; in water it is white; and in earth it is of many kinds, such as white and so forth. Color exists in three [elements]; taste is found in water as sweet; in earth it is of six kinds. Smell, according to the wise, is considered to be both non-fragrant and fragrant in earth. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 12.27–29). Thus [ends verses 9–11].
Now, the summary of the meaning already stated:
Thus, the elements beginning with earth, endowed with the aforementioned collection of odors and so forth,
are well-known to the world.
The meaning is that earth and the other elements are established in the world as the substrata for odors and so forth.

And because these elements possess qualities that are perceptible by the external senses of ourselves and others, their status as effects is established—just like a jar; therefore, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are established as their causes. Thus he says:
"The subtle elements [are known] through inference from them. (12)
Now, in order to demonstrate that by the very apprehension of the qualities (guṇas), the apprehension of the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is also established because it is non-different from them,
he says— first, to prove the non-separateness of the aforementioned elements from their qualities:
"The earth and the other elements are said to have a variegated nature and are not distinct from their qualities."
An example of that which is manifested through sequence is as follows: a painting [is seen] on a cloth, but [its details are not visible when the cloth is] rolled up. (13)
Earth and the other elements have been described. By implication, they are mutually distinct through their qualities such as odor and so forth;

moreover, they are seen to possess diverse natures due to differences in form, such as dry land, stones, mountains, rivers, and oceans. Therefore, these [elements] are manifested only sequentially, like the forms in a painting on a rolled-up cloth. For it is not the case that [the nature of] earth and the others—

The proximate essential nature, distinguished by the various intermediate forms that are being perceived, and the remote essential nature corresponding to it—all this can be grasped simultaneously; however, it is manifested by the sense organs and by inference only in succession. || 13 ||
What follows from this? To this he says:
"Because they are manifested sequentially, these [words] become the objects of the designation of qualifier and qualified, which is based on a distinction in cognition. (14)

These objects, such as the earth and so forth, because they are manifested through a sequence, become the objects of the various cognitions— consisting of qualifiers and qualificands— such as "this earth is fragrant," as well as the basis for the designation of their existence. || 14 ||
And in this regard:
"A cognition never arises without the apprehension of smell and the other [qualities];
for in the case of the earth, it arises even when water and the other [elements] are not apprehended. (15)
Therefore, earth is non-different from its qualities such as odor, yet it is distinct from water and the other elements;

for this reason, because no cognition of the earth— which is the substratum (dharmin) characterized by its specific qualities— ever arises when its specific qualities such as odor are not perceived, whereas [such a cognition does arise] in the case of other substances.

It certainly arises even when water and the other elements are not perceived. Therefore, earth is non-different from its qualities such as odor, but it is indeed different from water and the other elements.
He says that it should be understood in the same way regarding other elements as well:
"The wise should apply this very same reasoning to water and the other [elements]. (16)

[Objection: But surely, when in proximity to a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), a crystal gem (*sphaṭikamaṇi*) which assumes a red state is perceived even without the apprehension of the quality of whiteness; therefore, it is unestablished that the apprehension of the substratum (*guṇin*) is preceded by the apprehension of the quality (*guṇa*). To this, he says:
Shape as well as color—form is held to be twofold;
therefore, there is no lack of proof for the reason when the gem is obscured. (17)

For in this system, the form (*rūpa*) of substances—which consists of both color and shape—is accepted as being merely a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, even in the case of a crystal colored by a hibiscus flower, its perception occurs preceded by the perception of its shape, such as roundness or squareness, even in the absence of the perception of the quality of whiteness; thus, [this serves as] an example for the perception of a substance.
The fact that [the cognition] is preceded by the apprehension of qualities is already established; therefore, this reason is not unestablished (asiddha). || 17 ||

Having thus established that the elements serve as the instruments for experience, [the author] now demonstrates, by way of generalization, that the elements are effects—thereby further specifying the proof of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) previously mentioned in the verse beginning with "Now, the subtle elements [are proved] by inference from those" (Śloka 12): [He shows this] without specific designation: "First, the elements are effects... [and so forth].
Whatever reason is stated for establishing that the qualities (guṇas) are effects, it should be applied to establish the existence of a cause for all things from earth up to kalā. (18)
He will state that since the qualities (*guṇas*) are insentient and manifold, they must have a cause, just like a jar or similar objects.

Therefore, by that very same reason, the fact that earth and the other elements are effects is established. For instance, the group of thirty principles consisting of earth up to *kalā* [is an effect], because otherwise the observed diversity of experience could not be accounted for.

It has been stated that there exists a subtle body determined for each individual, and this is also heard in the scriptures. Therefore, since those elements such as earth and the rest are restricted to each person and are insentient, their multiplicity establishes that they must be preceded by a cause. || 18 ||

In that regard, since the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are not established as the material causes of the gross elements, the sequential order of earth and the other elements is established solely through the differentiation of their respective qualities; thus he says:
"The subtle elements [are so called] because of the successive increase by one [quality], such as sound, etc., due to the non-differentiation of those [qualities]."
They maintain that space and the other elements are the sources (yonis) of their respective attributes (dharmas) in due order. || 19 ||

This is the essential meaning here: the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), whose nature consists solely of sound with its specific qualities unmanifested, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of space; likewise, the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), situated below that and consisting of the nature of both sound and touch alone, is the cause of air; [and the subtle element of form] consisting of sound, touch, and form...
The subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) belongs to fire; the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*), consisting of sound, touch, form, and taste, belongs to water;
and the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), consisting of the five qualities beginning with sound and ending with smell, belongs to earth. As for the literal meaning of the words:

those [elements] which possess an increase of one additional quality each, starting with sound and so forth, like the ether and the others, are called "those possessing an increase of one additional quality each, starting with sound."

Because there is no distinction [in the unmanifest], and because the qualities (guṇas) are undifferentiated, they maintain that the sources— the material causes— of those elements such as space, which consist merely of the unmanifested specificities of sound and so forth, are the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and the rest; these are the origins for those very elemental entities (dharmis), such as ether and the others, which possess distinct qualities, according to the sequence of their creation.
The meaning is that, by descending through a sequence of increasing excellence of qualities, they bring about a progressively lower state even for their effects. || 19 ||
But how do these [pleasures] constitute a limb of enjoyment? To this he says:
"In all wombs, including those of mothers and so forth, their agency in producing and nourishing their own effects is determined to be the means for achieving the human goal. (20)

Since the performance of what has not been done and the augmentation of what has been done pertain to all the *upādānas*, it is established that the *tanmātras* and *māyā* and so forth— which are the sources of effects— constitute the state of being experience (*bhogatva*), because they produce the principles (*tattvas*) that are the means of experience and because they fulfill them. || 20 ||

Now, in order to demonstrate that the sense organs are also instruments for experience, he first states the proof for the existence of the organs of action: "The names of the genitals, feet, anus, mouth, and hands are indeed distinct [from those of the organs of perception], because their functions are pleasure, movement, excretion, speech, and grasping. (21)

"Emission" means the removal of impurities. The meaning is that the organs of action, such as the generative organ (*upastha*), are established as such because they are the causes of actions beginning with sexual pleasure.

He asks: "Are these organs merely the physical locations, such as the generative organ? and answers: "But in the Smṛti, it is taught that for each of the [five] actions, existence and non-existence depend upon them."
When their respective locations exist, these five are indeed the organs of action here.

For here, in some cases, even those yogis who occupy positions such as the "feet" (pādādi) and are devoid of the power of their respective sense organs are not seen to perform actions such as walking. Therefore, although those locations exist, it must be understood that the powers residing there—upon whose presence or absence the existence or non-existence of those actions depends—are themselves distinct from the five [perceptive] senses. For this very reason, they are the organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*).
The Naiyāyikas and others who do not accept this have been refuted. || 22 ||
If this were so, then because actions such as the raising of the creeper-like eyebrows would also be [counted as] *kriyā*, it would follow that there are infinite organs of action;
therefore, he says:
"By these actions, beginning with bliss (*ānanda*), which have been thus designated..."
Therefore, the organs of action [are five]; their infinity does not arise from the power of actions. || 23 ||

This fault would arise if we were to maintain that those [faculties] reside in only one part of the body; however, since they are accepted as pervading the entire body—just like the sense of touch—this activity of raising the eyebrows and so forth belongs to the hand alone, much like the function of the anus and other organs consists of excretion and the like. Thus, because activities such as the raising of the eyebrows are also included within [the functions of] bliss and the rest, there is no fault.

From their differentiation, the infinity of the sense organs is established here. Furthermore, by means of these very aforementioned primary actions—bliss and so forth—the five organs of action are established; thus, there is no infinity of the organs of action, though they receive various designations in different contexts.
There is no contradiction because of the specific basis [of the manifestation]. || 23 ||
Now he states the proof for the existence of the sense organs:
"In the perception of sound and other objects, there can be no action on the part of the person as agent without an instrument;
nor can there be action with only one instrument, since the requirement [for further instruments] does not cease. (24)

Since the apprehension of sound and the other objects is also an action, it is not logical for it to arise without an instrument, just like the act of cutting. Furthermore, these five actions do not all arise from a single instrument such as the ear; for the requirement of other instruments does not cease, since even when the ear—which is the instrument for apprehending sound—is present, the apprehension of touch and the other qualities still requires other instruments such as the skin.
The sense is that it is seen. || 24 ||
To the question "What are those instruments? he says:
"The instruments are hearing, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
And with the intention that these are inferred from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of sound and the other objects, he says:
The function of these [senses] is the mere observation of sound and so forth when sound and other objects are present. (25)

In the reading *sannibheti*, the meaning is that the senses, presided over by the mind, present to knowledge as its object an internal form that corresponds to external forms such as sound and so forth— forms determined by the intellect (*buddhi*). And the Person [perceives] that form, which has been presented by the senses and determined by the intellect, by means of the internal instrument called knowledge (*vidyā*).
We shall explain that [the self] "grasps. And it has been stated elsewhere:
"The person perceives the object determined by the intellect" (see footnote 2 on page 78 of the previous section). || 25 ||
Nor are these sense organs merely the physical locations such as the ear-cavity; rather, they are the powers residing therein.
For even when the locations are present, due to the force of karma, the cognition of sound and so forth does not arise if those powers are deficient. Thus he says:
"Do not think that these sense organs of the intellect are merely their locations."
Because, even when the locations exist, it is not perceived due to a deficiency. || 26 ||
Now, the proof of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is stated: Desire, exertion, and cognition are not established by the aforementioned means;
for their establishment, there must be internal instruments—namely, mind (manas), ego (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi). (27)

For here, since the principles such as earth and the rest are established by their own effects alone, there is no evidence for their being causes of further effects; moreover, it would follow that one must either deny the plurality of principles or accept them as non-existent. Therefore, those means of proof which establish desire and so forth are internal instruments known as mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*); thus is the establishment of the internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
In this context, by the word "will" (icchā), what is intended is volition (saṅkalpa) consisting of attentiveness, which is synonymous with one-pointedness. That is a function of the mind (manas).

Furthermore, "impulse" (saṃrambha) is effort (prayatna) belonging to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and "cognition" (bodha) is determination (adhyavasāya) belonging to the intellect (buddhi). This will be elaborated upon later. || 27 ||

He states that these internal and external organs serve as means for achieving the goals of the person (*puruṣārtha*) through mutual assistance: "The internal and external [organs], acting together, are the means for desire and so forth; like men carrying a palanquin, they [function] by the removal of one [organ] at a time. (28)

And for those who have turned inward and are realizing the true nature of consciousness, the activities such as desire and so forth no longer exist together with the intellect regarding external objects. (29)

Since both the internal and external organs, like men carrying a palanquin, become the means for actions such as desire when they act in concert— given that we observe determinations and so forth are preceded by the perception of external objects,
and because the apprehension of external objects is impossible without attention and the like— it follows that [the organs serve] the purpose of the conscious Self.

For those whose purpose is the attainment of what is called enjoyment, and whose internal organs (antahkarana) have turned inward— or, by the force of the word "ca," for those whose external organs (bahiṣkaraṇa) or either group of organs remain withdrawn— those activities such as desire, or cognitions of external objects like sound and so forth, do not arise because they are not means for achieving the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), just as follows:
When one of the two bearers of a palanquin departs from between them, the act of carrying it is no longer observed. || 28–29 ||
Here, he states the opinion of others: "Others maintain that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the vital breath (prāṇa), possessing manifest consciousness;
others, belonging to a certain school of Lokāyata, [hold it to be] the cause of life and so forth, by means of functions such as leading [the body]."
They claim that the internal organ is simply the internal wind called *prāṇa*, whose consciousness is manifested through a specific transformation of the elements (*bhūta*).
He states the refutation of this:
"Without efforts, that [internal organ] does not exist; what, then, would be the instrument for the accomplishment of those [efforts]? (30)
First, regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is of the nature of air (*vāyu*), its activity is observed to be preceded by effort due to its occasional occurrence. As they say:

"How could there be the impelling and drawing of the air without effort? (*Pravārttikā* 1.54). Therefore, since an effort consisting of exertion (*saṃrambha*) is established, there must necessarily be some instrument (*karaṇa*) [for it], and thus the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is established. And he will say:
"Excitement is a function of egoism" (verse 33). || 30 ||
Furthermore, since you have admitted that consciousness arises from this wind, you must state another instrument for that [arising]; thus he says:
"Tell me, what is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) for this burden of the outpouring of consciousness?"
Furthermore, its consciousness is clearly not manifest, because it is air, like external air. || 31 ||

The manifestation of consciousness in that which is insentient is not logical, because it would entail the consequence of consciousness manifesting in everything; therefore, this [body] does not possess consciousness, because it is air, like external air. || 31 ||

Having thus rejected the position that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is manifold, he states the proof for the existence of *manas* as distinct from the three previously mentioned internal organs:
"It is the cause of desire, it moves swiftly, and it impels the external deities."
And because of the impurity of his mind, the agent does not possess simultaneous cognition. || 32 ||

Because they shine (*dyotana*), the sense organs are called "deities" (*deva*); and by the word "cognition" (*mati*), knowledge regarding its respective objects is meant. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: for here, even though there is contact between the self and the objects of the senses, not all the senses function simultaneously; rather, only a certain one does so, and even that does not function at all times. Therefore, that instrument which [causes] its functioning—

The mind (manas) should be understood as that which is the cause of the attention consisting of volition (saṅkalpa), which is of the nature of His will, and which sets the external senses in motion. For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga-tantra* that "that mind has a twofold jurisdiction" (*dvidhādhikāri*), by virtue of its internal basis in the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) through volitions such as pleasure, and its external basis in the external senses.

"Because it always produces for the enjoyer the means of enjoyment through its own appropriate nature as the external organs, the capacity of the senses is further brought about by the volition residing within the self; therefore, that which is situated within is the internal organ, the mind. (Vijñānabhairava 18.81–82). Also, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The mind is the impeller of the gods, moving swiftly, and characterized by volition. (Vijñāna-bhāṣya)

(12.7) Thus it is said. Now, one might object: "In the tasting of a beautiful, very long *śaṣkulī* (sweetmeat) that is sweet, fragrant, of noble quality, and makes a crisp sound, the simultaneous arising of five cognitions is observed.
This is not so; for even there, the five cognitions arise with imperceptibly subtle sequences, just like the distinct manifestations of the hundred petals of a blue lotus.
For this very reason, it is said that this [power] moves swiftly. || 32 ||
The impulse of the ego (ahaṅkṛti) is the activator for the life-force (vāyu) to perform its fivefold functions;

it is the function of the ego that performs the five actions— such as leading [breath] in and leading it out— for the sake of life, that is, for the maintenance of the body, according to their respective specific modes of activity.

The effort characterized by impulsion (*saṃrambha*), which sets in motion the wind known as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth, is a function (*vṛtti*) of the *ahaṅkāra*; thus is the proof of the *ahaṅkāra*. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Then, from within the manifest [evolutes], there arose from the intellect (*buddhi*) the *garva* (ego-sense), the instrument of consciousness; through its impulsion, the five bodily winds exert themselves."
(Vi. 11.20). In this context, *praṇayana* is the upward and downward movement of the subtle body, which is the function of *prāṇa*.

*Apanayana* is the downward discharge of waste matter and so forth, which is the function of *apāna*. *Samānayana* is the equal distribution throughout all the limbs of food and such things that have taken the form of *rasa*; this is the function of *samāna*. *Vinamana* is the bending of the limbs, which is the function of *vyāna*. *Unnayana* is the lifting up of internal [substances].

The attainment of the state of phonemes by sound is due to the *udāna* breath; and it is stated [in the scriptures] that it performs five functions because of its predominance, as this wind is heard to be the agent of belching and so forth. As it is said in the venerable *Kālottara*: "Nāga is said to be in belching, Kūrma resides in opening the eyes, Kṛkara is in sneezing, Devadatta in yawning, and Dhanañjaya resides..."
"Even for one who has died in a cowherd settlement, it does not leave him. (10.12–13) Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, he states that the cognition in the form of the grasping-determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the subject as "I"— which appears as entirely distinct from the cognitions in the form of objective determinations such as "this is a jar" arising from the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*), and which remains of a single form even when grasping all objects— is indeed a function (*vṛtti*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
The cognition of one object is distinct from that of another. || 33 ||
The meaning is that the cognition consisting of the modification of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra-vṛtti) is distinct from the cognition of the object. || 33 ||

But surely, functions such as the apprehension of sound are the specific (asādhāraṇa) activities of the ear and the other senses, whereas "impulse" (saṃrambha) is a common (sādhāraṇa) activity of those very same organs; so what is the use of postulating a separate ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)? To this he replies:
"Impulse is not held to be a common function of the group of deities [the senses]."
For when any one of these is lacking, the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) arises. || 34 ||

Since it has been stated that when one among those performing a collective action is absent, that action does not arise, the meaning is this: even when there is a deficiency in those [factors], this surge of activity or the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) that nevertheless occurs is the effect of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) alone. || 34 ||

In this very context, in order to demonstrate that the groups of the cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), together with the mind (*manas*), arise from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), he says:
"And there are other groups of ego-sense, three in number, which give rise to the three classes [of faculties]."
Those named Taijasa and the others correspond respectively to the Sāttvika and other [guṇas]. || 35 ||

The three groups of ego (ahaṅkāra-skandhas), abounding respectively in sattva, rajas, and tamas, are known in succession as taijasa, vaikārika, and bhūtādi; their status as sāttvika and so forth is due to the predominance of the qualities of sattva and the rest. || 35 ||
Since, according to the principle that "the unmingled does not transform," there is also a commingling of other qualities among these, from what and of what is their origin? To this he says:
"Because the group of the sense-deities, together with the mind, is illuminating."
Therefore, he was born from the Sāttvika ego (ahaṅkāra), which was concordant with his own nature.
In this regard, he refutes the view of the Naiyāyikas by restating it:
"But others have maintained that the sense-faculties of the gods are material;
however, because there is no restriction regarding objects, [their existence] is not established from the reason itself. (37)

For they think as follows: since the sense organs have restricted objects—such as the ear, which perceives sound alone, and the skin, which perceives touch alone—they must be produced from the elements such as space (*ākāśa*), which serve as the substrata for sound and the rest.

If, however, they were derived from the *ahaṅkāra*, then because they would have a single cause, they would possess a single uniform nature; consequently, the restriction of each to its specific object could not be established.

This [position] is postulated by them on the basis of a reason that is simply unestablished (*asiddha*), because for them the restriction of objects—which would establish a restriction of nature—is unproven. For if the sense organs were restricted to specific objects, they would perceive only their own respective material causes (*bhūta*) accompanied by their qualities (*guṇa*). However, in reality, other substances as well as their qualities are perceived by the eye and the other senses.
They are grasped. || 37 ||
For instance:
the wind, together with the skin, perceives the four types of touch residing in the four substances, as well as substances in an indefinite manner, along with the wind itself. (38)
The tactile sense-organ (tvag-indriya), which is admitted to be composed of air, perceives earth, water, and fire along with the air, as well as the tactile qualities residing therein. || 38 ||
Furthermore: "There are three substances—the eye, those [substances], and indeed visible forms;
therefore, no fixed rule is postulated for the sense-faculties and their objects. (39)

He states another refutation: "Furthermore, because of the material nature of the restriction and the commonality of karma, cognitions would clearly not arise from the gods, nor [would they arise] in the inherent relation (samavāya) of embodied beings. (40)

If the restriction of the objects of the senses is accepted as a means of proving their material nature, then the cognitions of those categories— action, generality, and inherence— which you accept as distinct from the elements and the qualities, could not arise from them. (40)
As for what was also asked— how there can be a difference in the functions of the senses if they are equally derived from the *ahaṅkāra*—
that too will occur due to differences in their origin (*utpatti*), just as among the various products of sugarcane, such as molasses, sugar-candy, and granulated sugar. Thus,

even though the ears and other senses require specific determinants for the apprehension of sound and so forth, we maintain that it is indeed *karman* (past action) that bestows the objects of human purpose upon them.
He says that [the Lord] is intended to be the director:
"Furthermore, my birth as one possessed of ego-consciousness is not the cause for this regulation;
rather, that karma which bestows the goals of human life is the cause impelled by Him. (41)
We do not maintain that the state of being born from egoism alone is the cause for the restriction of objects; rather, the meaning is that it is action presided over by Śiva. || 41 ||
If it is accepted that sound is manifested in a portion of space distinguished by a bodily cavity,

then since the nostrils and other such cavities would also follow as being auditory organs, even the proponent of material (bhautika) sense organs must admit that karma— known as the "unseen force" (adṛṣṭa)— is the regulating factor that restricts the capacity to perceive sound to the auditory space alone.
Thus he says:

"Even by another [teacher], for the sake of avoiding contradictions with various scriptural passages, a cause has been postulated for the restriction of the experience of sound in the supreme ether; that [cause] is stated to be karma which bestows it. (42)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when the ether of the body (*khe kāye*) is postulated as the grasper of sound, then—out of fear of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that there would be hearing of various sounds simultaneously—the very ether of the auditory organ (*śravaṇākāśa*) must be restricted to the grasping of sound; thus, even by you, the "word of human purpose" (*puruṣārthapada*), namely *karman* (action), is accepted as the cause.

Thus he states that the organs of action are derived from ego-consciousness: "From the *vaikṛta* [ego] characterized by *rajas*, however, arises the group of the organs of action which perform actions;
for by this, the effect here conforms to its cause. (43)

Because *rajas* is the cause of activity, from the *ahaṅkāra*-aggregate known as *vaikārika*, which is characterized by *rajas*, the group of organs of action (*karmendriya*)—the cause of action—is born; for it is observed that the effect conforms to its cause. || 43 ||
For this very reason, since *sattva* is luminous (*prakāśa*), it is stated that the group of the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) arises from the *sāttvika* [aspect].

Otherwise, if one were to admit the arising of these two groups—which possess distinct natures—from a single cause, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), characterized by a lack of causal restriction, would ensue; thus he says:
An instability arising from transformation cannot be prevented once it has been established as originating from the *sattva* quality,
given that the categories of *sattva* and *rajas* have already come into being.
For this very reason:
"The group of subtle elements (mātrā-saṅgha) also arises from egoism (ahaṅkāra), being distinct from the two [preceding] groups;
it is to be manifested and is tāmasa, born from that which is designated as bhūtādi. (45)

Now he states that the intellect (buddhi) is the cause of determination and so forth: "Manifestation takes the form of the object; it does not exist anywhere except through the gateway of the [senses].
Because it is the ground for the manifestation of the consciousness of the Puruṣa, this manifestation is considered the function (vṛtti) of the intellect. (46)

This manifestation— consisting of the determination of external objects such as "this is a jar" through the door of the senses, or the independent internal manifestation of memory, intuition (*pratibhā*), and so forth, as well as the manifestation characterized by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) which will be described later— is called "cognition" (*bodha*), because it is the locus of the manifestation of the person's consciousness (*puruṣabodha*).

The activity of the intellect (*buddhi*) is to be understood as the mother [of the ego]. Therefore, the intellect is established by means of such signs as determination (*adhyavasāya*) and memory (*smṛti*).

As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "This illumination of the intellect, characterized by the cognition of objective states, is called 'consciousness' (*bodha*) because it serves as the ground for the manifestation of consciousness in the bound soul (*paśu*). (Vi. 11.8) || 46 ||
And he states that this awakening of the intellect (*buddhi*) is threefold:
"It consists of *kḷpti*, *mati*, and *smṛti*.
Among these, *kḷpti* means conceptualization (*kalpana*), which is to say, intuition (*pratibhā*). *Mati* is reflection (*manana*), which is knowledge (*jñāna*) or determination (*adhyavasāya*).
...up to...
Thus, concluding that the distinction of the internal organ is established through the difference in its effects—namely desire and so forth—he says:
"Having arisen as denoters of distinct objects, [the functions] called desire, exertion, and cognition; therefore, the internal organ is threefold. (47)

The meaning is that although there are intermediate distinctions among memory and the other [mental states], they constitute modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) because they have a single object by virtue of being cognizers; however, desire and the others are distinct modifications because they have different objects and thus have different causes. || 47 ||

Now, it may be argued that while the earth and other elements possess the status of being means of enjoyment (*bhoga-sādhana*) because they are objects of experience, and the sense organs possess it because they are the causes for perceiving those objects, the intellect (*buddhi*)—which arises in the self (*ātman*) from the contact between the senses and their objects—is not a means of enjoyment because its nature is that of pure cognition; rather, it is merely a quality of the self. To this, the Naiyāyikas and others respond: [the author] says:
If the possession of qualities is equal [in both cases], yet you maintain that some things are perceivable while the intellect itself is imperceptible—how fortunate indeed is your logic! (48)

This is the intended meaning: here, cognition is of two kinds—of the nature of determinate judgment (*adhyavasāyātmaka*) and of the nature of non-determinate intuition (*anadhyavasāyātmaka*). Of these, that which is of the nature of determinate judgment is the very essence of the Self (*ātman*), because it always appears solely in the form of the subject (*grāhakarūpa*).
However, that which is of the nature of non-determinate intuition is not the essence of the Person (*puruṣa*), because it appears as being subject to origination and cessation.

Because it is impossible for that which is eternal to have an impermanent nature, and because if it possessed such a nature, it would follow that it is impermanent; furthermore, an eternal [self] is not perceived, therefore it is not the nature of the person (*pums*). That which has this as its nature is *buddhi* (intellect), which produces the determination of objects and possesses the eight qualities such as the knowledge of *dharma*. And thus:

Because it consists of the determination of objects (*viṣayādhyavasāya*), because it exists as a state (*bhāvapratyaya*) endowed with the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) such as *sattva*, and because it is an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) by its very nature, the intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed something that is cognized, but it does not possess the quality of being a self (*ātman*). As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"In brief, the intellect—which takes the form of objects and consists of pleasure and so forth—is the object of enjoyment" (verse 13). And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows:

Intellect (buddhi) is also indeed an object of cognition, because it is associated with the qualities of sattva and so forth, just like earth and other elements. Furthermore, its status as an instrument is established—just like the sense organs—because it is the cause of the determination of objects; this has already been stated. || 48 ||

[Objection: But surely we also accept that entities such as *dharma* possess the quality of being attributes of the self (*ātma-guṇatva*). [Reply: That is incorrect, because it is impossible for them to be embellishments (*saṃskāraka*) of the self. To explain: first, the embellishment resulting from rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* cannot reside in the self, because the self is immutable (*avikāritva*), and because actions such as agriculture are not observed to be embellishments of the self; rather, they belong to the insentient [body].
Thus, that in which those [impressions] produce a latent trace (*saṃskāra*) is *buddhi*. The same should be said regarding the traces of knowledge and so forth;
for it is by the power of those very [traces] that an appearance is observed even when the object is non-existent, as in dreams, memory, and intuition. And therefore:
"The internal and external organs are the direct means for experience."
Since there is no enjoyment without that which is to be enjoyed, this is the means for enjoyment. (49)

The internal and external group of instruments (*karaṇagrāma*) is the direct means for experience (*bhoga*), which consists of the perception of pleasure, pain, and so forth, by the self (*ātman*). As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Experience for this person is sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and the like.
And that experience would not occur without objects of enjoyment such as garlands, sandalwood, and so on; therefore, [the instruments] are preceded by the grasping of those [objects].
The means for the determination of pleasure and so forth is also intended [to be established]. || 49 ||
He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration:
"Just as a king employs his soldiers here for the sake of victory, so does the atom employ the great elements (mahat) and the rest for the sake of cognition and other functions. (50)

Just as the king possesses agency in victory when it resides in his soldiers, so too is the agency of the person (puruṣa) asserted in regard to cognition and the like when they reside in the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties. 51.
Just as soldiers do not desire victory for their own sake, but rather as a means to achieve it,
so too do the principles beginning with Mahat [desire] for the sake of that [victory].
For it is certain that even for them [the organs], awakening and so forth do not constitute their own purpose.
Since the instruments (karaṇas) are insentient, their functions do not have their own purpose; rather, the sense is that they exist solely for the sake of the sentient Puruṣa. (50–52)
Therefore, the means for the functions beginning with cognition are the Great One (mahat) and the others. || 53 ||
Now he divides that which is to be experienced (bhogya):
"That which consists of the forms of delusion, suffering, and pleasure is called 'form' (rūpa); its existence is twofold.
The cognition of the Buddha is the supreme object of experience, and [the world] beginning with Māyā exists for that purpose. (54)

Because it is the cause of delusion (*moha*) and so forth through the manifestation of its own qualities, the category of phenomena consisting of form (*rūpa*), names (*saṃjñā*), and mental factors (*dharma*) takes on the aspect of delusion and the like;

likewise, the category of causal conditions such as accomplishment (*siddhi*) which is derived from that [category]—this twofold Buddhist cognition is the object of experience most proximate to the person. Since it follows from that [cognition] and exists for its sake, the world and other entities, beginning with *māyā*, are the locus of experience.
Because it is, through a succession [of causes], that which is to be enjoyed. || 54 ||
To the question "What is this called 'form' (rūpa)? he says:

The triad beginning with non-dharma, attachment, and the fourfold group beginning with dharma—consisting of tamas, rajas, and sattva—is considered form, born of that [mental] activity within the intellect (matau). (55)
The form known as unrighteousness (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya) is tamasic; attachment (rāga), which is synonymous with non-detachment (avairāgya), is rājasa;

and righteousness (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), detachment (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya) are sāttvika. Thus, this eightfold form exists in the intellect (buddhi) as a quality, produced from action (karman) and its material cause (upādāna). However, the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), bodies (śarīra), and so forth, arise through action alone acting as a cooperative cause (sahakārin).

It is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* and other scriptures that [the universe] has arisen directly and indirectly from the material cause known as Māyā. And these [two views]: "Liberation consists in absolute annihilation" and "Liberation consists in manifestation everywhere"— [The following verse follows: atyantocchedato muktāvabhivyakteśca sarvataḥ | muktāvasthādvayaṃ prāptuṃ vāñchadbhirvividhairjanaiḥ || 56 || tattadabhyupagantṛbhyo dīyate tattaduttaram | tathāpi naiva taddheturjñānaṃ vā kriyayā saha || 57 || tasmāttattvāntarajñānātkriyāto vā na mokṣaṇam | kiṃ tu svātmaparijñānādeva muktiḥ suniścitā || 58 || svātmano hi parijñāne svātmaivopādhiśūnyatām | prāpya muktimavāpnoti nānyatheti viniścayaḥ || 59 || This two-fold state of liberation is desired by various people who wish to attain it through either absolute annihilation or universal manifestation; therefore, answers are given to those who subscribe to each of those [views]. Nevertheless, neither knowledge nor action, even when combined, is the cause of that [liberation]. Thus, there is no liberation through knowledge of some other principle or through ritual action; rather, liberation is firmly established as occurring solely through the thorough realization of one's own Self. Indeed, upon the thorough realization of one's own Self, the Self itself attains a state free from limiting adjuncts and achieves liberation; it is not otherwise—this is the certain conclusion.
Because the Self is pervasive due to the cognition of cloth and other objects, its qualities are not [inherently] qualities.

Since even by others it is maintained that in liberation there is the absolute cessation of phenomena and so forth; since it is heard that in liberation the eternal, pervasive self-nature consisting of knowledge and action is manifested through its omnipresence;
and because the non-pervasiveness and non-universality of cognitions such as those of cloth—which consist of conceptual determination—are observed; [therefore, the soul is not momentary].

Therefore, non-eternal and non-pervasive qualities such as demerit (*adharma*) and the like cannot be attributes of the eternal and pervasive Self, because if they were inherent in it (*samavāya*), it would follow that the Self is subject to defects such as transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). Furthermore, these [qualities], beginning with demerit, arise from the Self in three varieties according to the distinctions of innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), acquired through discipline (*vainayika*), and natural (*prākṛta*). As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
The atom possesses innate, acquired, and natural qualities.
For those whose minds are illuminated by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of distinguished qualities, the innate quality (*sāṃsiddhika-guṇa*) shines forth even after the fall of the body, just as before.

The acquired quality (*vainayika-guṇa*) shines forth from the world, common understanding, teachers, and scriptures; this acquired quality is earned through the disciplined activity of mind, speech, and body.
"In its union with the body, the primordial [consciousness] becomes manifest, like the cognition of dreams and so forth" (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.26–29). || 56 ||

And thus, he states the distinctions among the fruits resulting from these three types of factors (dharma and so forth): "For these, the results are, respectively: downward rebirth, bondage, and obstruction; heaven, liberation, and the state of primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as obstruction. (57)
Existence, the fault of the station, obstacle, non-transcendence of enjoyments, subjugation, upward abiding, possessing right vision, and lack of longing for enjoyments are the fruits. (58)
In the form of one's own contemplation, there is an obstacle; in the spontaneously accomplished form, the fruit [is attained];
and in the form of the ordinary person to be trained, there is a collection of the fruits previously mentioned. || 59 ||
From the *vainayika* and *prākṛta* types of ignorance, such as *adharma* and the rest, the fruits are, respectively, downward rebirth and so forth;
from the *sāṃsiddhika* type, however, they are rebirth and so forth. Among these, "downward rebirth" (*adhogati*) is the attainment of hell;
"bondage" (*bandha*) is the conceit of self in what is not-self and so forth; "transmigration" (*saṃsṛti*) is the attainment of animal births and the like; and "liberation" (*mukti*) is—
Liberation upon seeing [the deity] (*darśanāntaramokṣa*), because supreme liberation is stated in the *Mokṣakārikās* to be the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

The state of primordial nature (*prakṛtibhāva*) is absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*). Existence (*bhava*) is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Offense against one’s station (*sthānāparādha*) is the humiliation of one’s own position. Non-transcendence of enjoyment (*bhogānatikrama*) is the desire for enjoyment. The upward abiding of those under control (*vaśya*) refers to those who are subject to control.

The presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consists in abiding in the state situated beneath one's own level. The possession of right vision (*saddṛṣṭi*) is the application of correct knowledge regarding each respective object.
The rest is easy to understand. (57–59)
Having thus reflected upon the states of being, he explains the conditions:
"The realization of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower is now accomplished through the collection of dharma and the rest, from which the limbs are merely smeared with passion. (60)
For here, the eight entities beginning with *dharma* are said to exist within the intellect (*buddhi*) as latent impressions (*vāsanā*). As it is said:

"Because they cause the *liṅga* (the subtle body) to come into being, they are proclaimed as *bhāvas* (entities)" (Pauṣkaratantra). These very same [entities], having reached a state of excellence and attained a gross form that has become an object of experience, are called *pratyayas* (cognitions/objects of cognition) because they bring about the perception of transmigrating beings.

They are so called because it has been said: "They cause the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) to be cognized; therefore they are known as 'cognitions' (*pratyaya*). Consequently, from the fourfold states such as virtue (*dharma*), which are characterized by *sattva* and joined with passion (*rajas*) and inertia (*tamas*), perfection (*siddhi*) arises through detachment (*vairāgya*). And that perfection consists in the thorough awakening regarding the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*) primary matter (*pradhāna*), and the Knower (*jña*), the Puruṣa, as well as the knowledge concerning them.

Knowledge itself, when it has reached a state of excellence, is called *siddhi* (accomplishment). And it has been said: "That cognition which has as its objects the Spirit (*puruṣa*), Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), and so forth, is here [defined as] *siddhi*" (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 11.2). In that regard, when there is the awakening of the intellect (*buddhi*) concerning the manifest and the unmanifest, the Spirit (*puruṣa*), being utterly distinct as the illuminator of those [objects], shines forth by itself; as they say: "Then for the Seer..."
"Abiding in its own nature" (Yoga Sūtra 1.3); it is not by being illumined by the intellect, for that would entail defects such as its becoming an object of experience (*bhogya*).

As he will state in the *Mokṣakārikās*: "If the person (*pumān*), which is subject to transformation, were to become an object of experience when it falls within the range of that [intellect]" (verse 105).

Contentment, which arises from the triad beginning with sin and is conjoined with the forms of merit and so forth, consists in the cognition that one’s purpose has been achieved when the grasping of a self exists. (61)
From the triad of *adharma* and the other [qualities] when slightly mixed with the *sāttvika* qualities such as *dharma*, *tuṣṭi* (contentment) arises.

And that *tuṣṭi* occurs when, through the previously mentioned *siddhi* consisting of knowledge of the elements (*bhūta*) and subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there is a grasping of the self according to the nature described in those respective systems; this happens even for one who has not yet achieved his goal, due to detachment from lower objects.

The cognition arising in the form "I have accomplished my purpose" is called contentment (*tuṣṭi*). As it is heard [in the Mṛgendratantra]: "Contentment is that thought of one who has not yet accomplished his purpose, 'I am one who has accomplished his purpose'" (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 11.2). || 61 ||
Born from the triad beginning with unrighteousness (adharma) and colored by a trace of passion (rāga),
incapacity is the lack of power regarding auspicious [actions] and so forth, due to a deficiency of the deities.

Here, by the word "auspicious" (śubha), the operation of the sexual organ and the resulting pleasure are meant. The incapacity consisting of impotence, deafness, and so forth, which arises from the deficiency of those [organs] or from the deficiency of the body characterized by them, is this "inability" (aśakti); it results from the *tāmasa* category slightly mixed with the *rājasa*. And it has been said: "Incapacity is *tāmasa* because of the absence of activity and because of its nature as suffering."
"Even in the case of the Rajas quality, its presence in the effect is seen as residing in the cause" (Mṛcchakaṭikā-vivaraṇa 11.6). Thus [ends verse 62].
Therefore, cognition that does not correspond to reality arises from a state free from passion; when slightly permeated by factors such as dharma, the error becomes manifest. (63)

Therefore, from that group characterized by *tamas* and devoid of *rajas*, there arises—due to the presence of even a trace of *sattva*—the misconception (*viparyaya*) consisting of the apprehension of things as they are not; this is characterized by *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*. As it is heard:
"When the intellect is elsewhere due to some slight commonality, it is another [form of] misconception" (*Mṛgendra-vṛtti* 11.3). || 63 ||

Thus, having spoken very briefly, he concludes the discussion on the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi*) which consists of the abstract categories (*bhāvapratyaya*): "This quality of the intellect has been stated in brief;
the detailed expansion (*prapañca*) of these abstract categories is shown at length in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures."
And since this has been elucidated by us in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*, it should be understood from that very source; however, for fear of excessive length, it is not written here.
And this [world] is enjoyed by consciousness;
the remainder [of the sense] is "because it is an object of enjoyment."
It establishes its very state of being an object of enjoyment:
"And its status as an object of enjoyment is well-established, since it is experienced once it has arisen. (64)
Furthermore, that experience, as an object of enjoyment, sufficiently points toward an enjoyer.

For this cognition of the Buddha, its nature is solely that of being enjoyed (*bhogyatva*), due to its connection with arising and passing away; it does not possess the nature of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).
This is because it has been stated that [the enjoyer] is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as being eternally stable in the form of the grasper (*grāhaka*). || 64 ||
And for this reason:
because in this world, the desired establishment [of an object] is not achieved without a prover (sādhayitṛ). || 65 ||

For here, since this Buddhist cognition—which has been accepted as the enjoyer by the Buddhists who maintain that consciousness consists of intellect—is unstable and thus insentient like a jar or other such objects, it is impossible for it to be the enjoyer of the fruits of karma that arise at a later time; furthermore, it is [insentient] because it is an object of enjoyment, as previously stated. Therefore...
Experience (*bhoga*), which consists in the perception of the pleasure and so forth of various objects, establishes the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
For the accomplishment of the act of experiencing is not possible without an enjoyer who performs it, since experience itself is an action.
The sense is that the self is established by its being the agent of that [experience]. "Desired" (*samīhitā*) means "intended" (*abhīṣṭā*). || 65 ||
Here, an objection is raised: "The validity of inference is not established without corroboration by perception;
for in this case, the fire inferred by means of smoke was previously present and is now being perceived, and thus that inference [is validated]."
Corroboration by other means of valid cognition is observed; for this very reason, its validity is established.

The Buddhists argue that, just as in the case of smoke and so forth, no deviation from the probandum is observed in the case of the wheel-peak and other such [inferences], and since here too one perceives only cognition whose nature is experience, and because no difference in form between the knower and the cognition is perceived, even the inference of a "consumer" (bhoktṛ) from "consumption" (bhoga) lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge due to the suspicion of deviation; thus, there is no proof of a self distinct from cognition.
As for what they say—"We perceive this single nature of consciousness as a manifestation (*vivarta*) in various forms such as sugar, poison, and so forth;
let names be assigned to it as one pleases"—that is incorrect, as he says: "With what could that which is seen be corroborated, by virtue of which it might possess validity? (66)

The intended meaning is as follows: since experience (*anubhava*), which consists of the perception of objects—that is, enjoyment—appears with stability even during states such as deep sleep when external objects are absent, by virtue of having only the internal touch of the body as its object;

therefore, it is said that the Self, whose nature is the subject (*grāhaka*), is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) as being stable. Nor is it the case that...
It is reasonable to superimpose stability upon momentary cognition because of the contradiction of an action occurring within itself. As for what was also said—
that whatever exists is momentary because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity for that which is non-momentary— that too is not so,
because even a non-momentary object such as a jewel manifests objects like a jar and so forth in a successive manner.

This is because it is established by experience that various objects located in a single house are manifested simultaneously; furthermore, for that which is momentary and perishes at the very moment of its arising, there is an incapacity to perform an action that must be accomplished over multiple moments. These and other points have been demonstrated in detail by the Ācāryas in the *Śrīmanmataṅgavṛtti* and other works. || 66 ||
Therefore, even though the self is established through its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is stated by way of granting that it might be inferable:
"In this case, there is no corroboration of perception by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
here, perception does not depend upon corroboration by another means of valid cognition."
Because it possesses validity by virtue of generating a cognition of an object not yet apprehended, even in the absence of corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As they say:
"A means of valid cognition is that which makes known an object not yet apprehended.
But how then is there no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as the hub of a wheel? To this he says:
The exclusion of deviation [of the reason] is established through positive and negative concomitance. || 67 ||

When a relationship characterized by invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between a sign such as smoke and its object has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), no deviation (vyabhicāra) is observed in that case, just as with well-discriminated smoke in relation to fire. However, in the case of that which is produced from the top of a wheel and so forth, there is a misconception of "smokeness" due to a lack of discrimination regarding its true nature. Consequently, even here, in all instances of action...
Because an action is observed to be preceded by an agent, the enjoyer is inferred from the act of enjoyment. || 67 ||
He states that even for you, since the activity of effects and so forth is established in your own body as being preceded by intelligence,

the intelligence in another's body is inferred by means of inference— even without corroboration from other means of valid cognition— on the grounds that "if the property of the body were the means of knowledge, then intelligence would be accepted as its cause."

The meaning is that when the bodily property consisting of movement and so forth is the means of cognition—that is, the logical reason—then by means of that, the cognition which is its cause is established in another body. As they say: "Having observed an action preceded by cognition in one's own body, because of the perception of it elsewhere, cognition is known [to exist there as well]."

And for this reason, with the intention that the existence of an enjoyer is established by the impossibility of accounting for experience otherwise—just as the sense organs such as the eye are established by the impossibility of accounting for the perception of form and so forth—he says:
"From this inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), there is the validity of another [means of knowledge] as well. (68)
The validity of inference has been established;
as for what was stated by the Cārvākas— "Let there be an enjoyer,
but that [enjoyer] is merely the body, which consists of a collection of transformations of the four perceptible elements, earth and so forth"— it is precisely that [body].
The manifestation of consciousness occurs through a specific transformation, just as the power of intoxication is manifested through the modification of substances such as fermenting yeast;

furthermore, activities such as enjoyment are observed through the force of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other winds. It is not something other than that [consciousness], because it is not perceived by direct perception.
As they say: "When a visible cause is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is not logical."
He states that even this has been refuted:
"For this very reason, the conscious [self] is established as the enjoyer of the cognition of the intellect. (69)
It is not logical that there should be a mere aggregation of earth and the other elements.

This is the intended meaning: since even the body is observed to be an object of experience—internally by way of pain and so forth, and externally by way of touch such as softness or hardness—it is not reasonable for it to possess consciousness, just like a jar or similar objects; therefore, the Self must be its experiencer.
"He is accomplished," thus [it is said]. || 69 ||
And its possession of consciousness is not established by any means of valid cognition; thus he says: "By what means of knowledge have you determined that it possesses consciousness? (70)

Now, since consciousness is observed only when the elements that constitute the body—composed of semen and blood—are present, and is not observed in their absence, it follows that consciousness is identical with the body; to this, he replies:
"Even if [the body] exists, there is inconclusiveness."

Since consciousness is not observed in a corpse, in an embryo, or even when the elements that constitute the body are present, consciousness does not consist of the body; therefore, the doctrine that the body is the self is not supported by valid means of knowledge. Thus he says:
"Therefore, it is like the cry of a crow."
And because it is an object of enjoyment, it is insentient; thus he says:
"Sugar and other such things, being objects of enjoyment, are observed to have unmanifest consciousness. (71)
Let it be that [the soul] is similar to molasses and the like because it is an object of enjoyment through its shadow;
for molasses and such things, being made objects by the soul—the self—through its shadow, which is consciousness in the form of experience, are never seen to have manifest sentience. Therefore...
The body, though consisting of a collection of elements, is indeed insentient because, as stated previously, it is made an object of experience through its being grasped as something to be enjoyed;

therefore, its status as an enjoyer is not tenable. Furthermore, if the body alone were sentient, then because it perishes through repeated transformation, it would be impossible for what was experienced during childhood to be remembered in old age, and so forth, as explained in detail.
This position has been refuted by us in the *Śrīman-mṛgendra-vṛtti-dīpikā*. (71)

Now, the proponents of the sentience of the senses (indriyacaitanika) claim that the capacity for being an enjoyer belongs only to the senses, which are distinct from the body, and not to anything else; to show that this is incorrect, he says:
"By virtue of their being objects of enjoyment and being instruments, the nature of the senses is definitively established. (72)
Therefore, the Puruṣa is the enjoyer because he is devoid of consciousness, whereas his nature is pure awareness.

As stated previously, since the sense organs also serve the purpose of enjoyment and are thus objects of experience, their lack of sentience is unavoidable—just like weapons and other such tools—because they function as instruments; consequently, they do not possess agency, but rather...

[The agency belongs] to the Self alone, whose nature is consciousness. For it is logical that agency belongs to that very [Self] alone, as it is the cause for the engagement and withdrawal of all other causal factors (*kāraka*).
As they say: "He who is the lord over the causal factors in both engagement and withdrawal—whether inactive or active—he is the one truly called the 'agent' among causal factors. (72)
The experience of the enjoyer is the manifestation of consciousness colored by the reflection of the object of experience.

The experience of the enjoyer is simply the manifestation of consciousness colored by the form—the shadow—of the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of pleasure and so forth. As it is said in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*: "The experience of this person is sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and the like. (73)
And at that time:
through its connection with consciousness, the insentient appears as an object of experience for the conscious;
likewise, even the insentient, which consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), appears as if conscious due to its intimate contact with the consciousness of that Self.
This has also been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "The subtle body (liṅga), though insentient, appears as if it were sentient" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 20).
And thus, by way of the objects of enjoyment, there is a mutual relationship between the fetters and the bound souls. (74)

The reflection of both conscious and unconscious objects shines forth intensely. For an object of enjoyment, presided over by the mind (*citta*), presents itself as an object of experience for the self (*ātman*) through the group of cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*); and the person (*puruṣa*) perceives that which has been determined by the intellect (*buddhi*). As they have said [in the second verse on page 78 of the earlier work]: [The text continues: "When the intellect, having assumed the form of the object, presents it to the self, the self, though pure, appears as if possessing consciousness. This is because the intellect, being non-conscious, cannot perceive the self; yet, when the intellect is colored by the reflection of the self, it becomes capable of perceiving objects. Thus, the intellect, like a mirror, reflects the self and the objects, and the self, in turn, perceives the intellect as its own object.
