Therefore, the self, though inherently pure, appears to be endowed with consciousness due to this proximity. This is the nature of the relationship between the seer and the seen. Thus ends the second verse.

See the *ṭippaṇī*. — "The *puruṣa* perceives the object determined by the intellect (*buddhi*). Consequently, because it is of the nature of luminosity, through the medium of the intellect—which stands in the place of a mirror and consists of the awareness of objects termed "experience"—there occurs the connection between the *ātman*s as enjoyers and the bonds (*pāśa*s) which have transformed into the form of objects to be enjoyed.

When the two shadows—one sentient and one insentient—are reflected, their adherence to each other's forms is merely a close proximity that appears, for the most part, as a single form. For this very reason, there arises among transmigrating beings the delusion of the Self and so forth in what is not the Self and so forth.
However, it is said that when they possess the knowledge of the discrimination between them, there is dissolution into *prakṛti*. And that alone is liberation for the Sāṃkhyas. (74)
And for this reason:
"The enjoyment in the object of enjoyment is like the reflection of the moon, the Lord, in water. (75)

For the Lord, the all-pervading Self, that very experience is the object of enjoyment; it is the manifestation of consciousness, distinguished by the reflection [of the intellect], within the cognition of the intellect—which consists of its own determination—just as the reflection of the moon appears in water. Because the lunar orb is insentient and gross, it serves here merely as an illustration for the manifestation of a specific form. Therefore, the sentient being possesses the status of an enjoyer.
It should be understood that agency belongs to the person alone, and not to insentient objects of experience such as the intellect and so forth. || 75 ||
Is it not the case that agency consists in the penetration of action? If that were to belong to the person (*puruṣa*), he would be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitā*).

For the person is changeless; therefore, he possesses no agency, but rather Prakṛti alone does. For prior to the knowledge of discrimination, she displays herself to him as an object of enjoyment in the form of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth; this is called "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*). But when that [knowledge] occurs—

Therefore, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that liberation is the cessation [of nature] and is denoted by the word "liberation. As they have said: "Just as a dancer, having exhibited herself to the audience, withdraws from the stage, so too does Nature (prakṛti), having manifested herself to the Spirit (puruṣa), withdraw."
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 59). To this he says:

"Because of the fear of transformation, when enjoyment is not desired by the Spirit (puṃs), the non-distinction between the enjoyer and the liberated [Spirit] follows as something difficult to avoid. (76)

This is the intended meaning: here, agency (*kartṛtva*) does not consist in the actual engagement in action (*kriyāveśa*), but rather in the mere possession of the capacity for action. For instance, just as iron moves due to the proximity of a magnet, so too the engagement in action—consisting of motion and the like—is observed in the body and other such things simply through the proximity of the Self. Consequently, in the case of experience (*bhoga*), which consists in being made an object of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, there is no risk of the Person (*puruṣa*) undergoing transformation (*pariṇāma*); rather, [agency belongs to the instruments].

[The cognition of the object] consists precisely in making that [object] the focus through being intent upon it. However, in your position, since the person is inherently pure, even if such intentness were not admitted, the unavoidable consequence would be that there is no distinction between the enjoyer and the liberated one;
for both would be identical in their state of being independent [of objects]. || 76 ||
But has it not been stated that primordial nature (*prakṛti*), being engaged in the service of another, acts for that purpose? As they say:

"Just as the flow of milk from the insentient [cow] is for the sake of the growth of the calf, so the activity of the primary matter (*pradhāna*) is for the sake of the liberation of the person (*puruṣa*)" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 57). To this, he says:
And the activity of the *pāśas* for the sake of the person’s goal has been refuted.

This is the intended meaning: because the *pradhāna* is insentient, its activity toward the *puruṣa* is not logical, since even things such as milk are observed to be active only when presided over by a sentient being, such as a cow; furthermore, wind, water, and so forth are also included within the scope of this argument.

Even if one accepts that [the Self] is active, activity toward that which is independent is not logical. Or, if activity were directed toward the independent, it would follow that it would also operate in the case of the liberated (mukta). Consequently, since desire is attributed to the bound self, there is exertion for the sake of experience; yet, if no modification (vikāra) is admitted in the Self, then experience itself is not tenable in that regard—thus he says:
If the enjoyer remains unmodified, enjoyment is not possible, just as it is not for one who is liberated. || 77 ||

Is it not the case that non-discrimination (*aviveka*) alone is the cause for the activity of *pradhāna*? However, when there is knowledge of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, [the *pradhāna*] does not proceed toward him because its mandate has ceased. Therefore, there is no lack of distinction between the bound and the liberated. As they say: "It is my conviction that nothing is more subtle than *prakṛti*; once she has been seen [by the *puruṣa*], she does not present herself for sight again."
"Of the person" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 61); this is incorrect, because in your own position, since the person is pure, non-discrimination is impossible;

furthermore, if non-discrimination were causeless, it would follow that there would be an absence of discrimination at all times. Therefore, we shall explain that even on the grounds of the impossibility of explaining non-discrimination otherwise, its impurity, passion, and so forth must be admitted. || 77 ||

If this is so, then since the self is admitted to be by nature ignorant due to its impurity, and to undergo modification through becoming a knower by means of association with the body and other factors, it follows that it would be subject to impermanence because of its connection with a different state of being; thus, he raises the objection of the opponent's view:
"If [the self] were impermanent due to being subject to modification..."
The word "enjoyer" is to be supplied as the subject. He refutes [this objection]:
he does not consider [the world] to be produced by illusion (māyā).

The implication is that you do not recognize the specific distinction being made through illusion by means of its own effects, namely via the subtle and gross bodies; therefore, the intended meaning is that there is no fault such as impermanence and so forth.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"And because it attains the manifestation of its own nature, there is neither modification nor destruction. (78)

We do not maintain that the Self is of an insentient nature, as the Naiyāyikas and others do; rather, its very essence is consciousness (*jña-svabhāva*). However, because that nature is not manifested in the absence of connection with the body and so forth, it is understood to be obstructed by some beginningless [factor], and we shall explain that this is indeed *mala*. Consequently, through *māyā* and the *kalās* and other [categories]...

By means of its own functions, through the removal of impurity (mala), only a partial manifestation of the Self's true nature is produced. However, when the impurity has reached maturity, the [Self's] capacity regarding all objects is manifested by the power of Śiva known as initiation (dīkṣā). Therefore, there is neither modification nor perishability for this [Self]. || 78 ||
And for this [Self],
attachment to the substrate of objects of enjoyment does not arise from the aforementioned cause because of its transparency;
therefore, even the attachment produced by the substrate of objects of enjoyment is a manifestation of this [Self] in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Because it is transparent like crystal and possesses the nature of luminosity, [the reflection occurs] not from the previously mentioned cause called "transformation" (pariṇāma). And it has been stated that even this coloring by the object is simply the mind's taking that object as its own, due to its being intent upon it.
Therefore, he states that although there is repeated transformation of the body, which is the object of experience, there is no transformation of the experiencer:
"The person (pudgala) is not subject to transformation through the transformation of the body. (79)

The meaning is this: since it is insentient and an object of experience due to its transformation, like the intellect (*buddhi*), if one were to admit its transformation as well, it would follow—just as in the case of the intellect—that it must be both an object of experience and insentient.
In this regard, having set forth the opponent's view, he refutes it:
"For consciousness is either a quality, or knowledge, or inherence, or else by means of that [inherence]. (80)
It is not logical that the nature of the *puruṣa* is anything other than this.

For the Naiyāyikas and others maintain this view: the self (*ātman*) is by nature insentient (*jaḍa-svabhāva*); through its conjunction with the mind (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*), knowledge arises as an inherent quality (*guṇa*) within it. That alone constitutes its consciousness (*caitanya*), and not any other state of being inherently conscious (*jña-svabhāvatva*).
That is incorrect, because if it were insentient, it would be incapable of the inherence of knowledge, just like a jar or other such objects. || 80 ||

[Objection: Surely there exists here a regulating factor called *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), which acts as the regulator such that knowledge arises as inherent (*samaveta*) in the person alone—being in the same substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as the action—and not elsewhere, such as in a jar, which is in a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*). To this, he says:
"The regulator is that knowledge resides only in the sentient being (*nārī*), and not elsewhere. (81)
Action (karma) also is not tenable as a regulator here, since it resides elsewhere.

It has been stated that action—such as agriculture and the like—is merely a refinement of primordial nature (prakṛti) and not a refinement of the self (ātman), because that would entail the consequence of the self being subject to modification. Therefore, even that cannot serve as a regulator in this context.
And therefore, because of the inherence of consciousness, the self is established as having the very nature of consciousness; thus he says:
"The wise hold that delusion is not a different entity from those things whose nature is delusion. (82)
Likewise, consciousness (*citi*) is not a different entity from conscious objects;

for since knowledge, which is of the nature of consciousness, is an attribute of the self, it follows that upon the destruction of the attribute, the substratum itself would also be destroyed due to its non-difference from that attribute. Therefore, the self must be admitted to be eternally of the very nature of consciousness. And of that [self]...
It has been stated that because they are veiled by impurity (*mala*), the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth are established as its manifestors.

Furthermore, he says that the three "sheaths" (*kañcuka*)— known as *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *rāga*— which serve as auxiliaries (*sahakārin*) in the activity of experience (*bhoga*) by acting as the agent, the instrument, and the colorer (*rañjaka*), will be explained later after the discussion on *prakṛti* and the means (*sādhana*).
The agent, the instrument, and the object of enjoyment; and the three [factors] that cause passion for what is above. 83.
The function of this experiencer will be taught later in relation to primordial nature (prakṛti).

Having thus established the enjoyer by way of incidental discussion, he now states that from the intellect (buddhi) itself arises the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is the subject at hand: "There is another distinct aggregate of the intellect which gave birth to the ego-sense. (84)

The qualities (*guṇas*) by which [the effects] are produced have been observed in the case of intuition (*pratibhā*) and the rest; for that reason, it is observed that in the operations of that intellect, such as intuition and so forth, the qualities are the producers of the effect through mutual suppression and through their union as a substrate, according to the method already stated, as it has been said: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the source text.*

The Sāṃkhyas state: "The guṇas function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 12). Therefore, a portion of the *skandha*—which is the cause of the determinative function (*adhyavasāya*) belonging to the intellect (*buddhi*) alone—becomes associated with the guṇas and produced the *ahaṅkāra*. Consequently, according to the principle that "a single [guṇa] is not a producer," it is only when the guṇas are mutually combined that they act as producers; and this is likewise the case in all instances.

They exist within all objects; the designation of them as "sāttvika" and so forth, however, is due to the predominance of *sattva* and the other qualities in those objects—this is the intended meaning. || 84 ||
And because it is the direct effect of the *guṇas*, the connection with the *guṇas* exists in this [Mahat] just as the connection with the form of clay exists in jars and other objects; thus he says:
"Therefore, that first transformation is appropriately attributed to the *guṇas* therein. (85)
"But the fixed arrangement [of their functions] is due to emergence and suppression.
For it has been stated that the qualities (guṇas), arising in that [intellect] by way of mutual suppression in a fixed order, produce success and so forth.
If this is so, then since the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) also possesses the qualities, let its origin likewise be from the qualities alone; therefore, he says:"
O learned one, do not prattle that this same logic applies to the ego as well. (86)
Because they are mutual modifications, this [defect] also applies to the subtle elements (*tanmātras*).

Since all principles from the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) down to the gross elements (*bhūta*) are mutual modifications—and thus, as previously stated, are modifications of the *guṇas*—the defect does not apply to the ego alone, but also to the subtle elements; the word "also" (*api*) indicates that it likewise applies to the group of sense organs and the group of gross elements.

The connection with qualities indeed persists, just as the form of clay persists in jars, potsherds, and so forth; however, there is no fault, because it is not the case that everything arises directly from the qualities themselves. || 86 ||
Now, what are those qualities (guṇas), and by what operations is their accomplishment achieved? To this he says:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities of the intellect (dhi) which serve as its causes. (87)
Those who, by means of the constraints of manifestation and activity, have extended the connection with the Puruṣa;

those who, as previously stated, through the medium of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, created—and even now continue to create—the objects of the Puruṣa’s experience in the form of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) and the like at the beginning of creation; for them, the *guṇas* are the cause even of the intellect. And these...

Because they are never separated from one another, reality is indeed one. As it is heard: "Though there are three qualities, they are nevertheless a single reality because of their inseparability" (Mṛgendrāgama-vṛtti 10.21). Therefore, by virtue of being the cause of the intellect (*buddhi*), the existence of *sattva* and the other qualities is established through their functions known as illumination, activity, and restraint. These have been demonstrated primarily for the sake of clarity, though others—such as stability, fortitude, and so forth—are also present.
For it is heard in the scriptures that qualities such as valor and cruelty, as well as effects such as lack of interest and dullness, [arise from these causes]. || 87 ||
Now, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that it is the guṇas themselves that exist eternally under the name of *pradhāna*; [the author] says this is incorrect:
"Even though they are insentient, [they are designated as such] because of their connection with the number 'many'. (88)

It is accepted that these [elements] are preceded by a cause, just like a pot or other such objects. Since they possess multiplicity due to their connection with the number "many," it follows from this multiplicity and their lack of consciousness that their status as effects is established, just like a pot or similar things. || 88 ||
To the question "What is their substrate? he says:
"That which is the substrate of the qualities (guṇas) is designated as Nature (prakṛti). (89)
That in which [the qualities] abide without differentiation, yet emerge when impelled by Śiva;

wherein the qualities, existing in a subtle state without differentiation, become manifest as gross through their respective functional divisions by the instigation of Śiva—that is *prakṛti*. By the phrase "impelled by Śiva," it is indicated that because she is insentient, her activity does not proceed with independence.

[The author] demonstrates this: we shall explain that because this [māyā] exists within the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) for each individual person, it possesses multiplicity and is therefore an effect (*kārya*).

(89) Now, since the Person (*puruṣa*), when joined with the fivefold sheath (*kañcuka*) beginning with *kalā*, is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), he attains the state of being a male (*puṃstva*) through union with *puṃs-mala*.

Therefore, for the sake of its purification during initiation (*dīkṣā*), although it is recited in the Āgamas as being above the *prakṛti-tattva*, because it is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and conscious (*cetana*), [it is not included there].

Since the state of being an enjoyer and the state of being an instrument of enjoyment are not possible [for the Self] alone, he disregards that [Self] and, in order to establish the previously mentioned principle of attachment (*rāga-tattva*) as the very factor that causes coloring, says:
"Having attained the experience of the object of enjoyment, attachment toward that object of enjoyment arises. (90)

For the sake of its accomplishment, there arises in him passion (*rāga*), which is the coloring of enjoyment. For in this state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), upon seeing an object of enjoyment, an attachment toward it occurs in the person (*puruṣa*). And that [attachment] does not arise without a cause, because otherwise it would follow that it exists even in the state of liberation. Therefore, for that person, from that attachment...
For the sake of accomplishment, passion that generates a longing for enjoyments must be admitted. || 90 ||
Herein is the opponent's intention:
"Sattva, when joined with rajas and tamas, is that which causes attachment to sense objects. (91)
Therefore, for a person, that which has arisen from the Buddha is meaningful, while anything else is useless.
He [the author] refutes this: "In his doctrine, that which is to be enjoyed has arisen; he who is attached to it [is the one who attains it]. (92)
That passion is to be understood as distinct [from the senses]; for this is indeed a defect even with respect to form (rūpa).

This is because the three qualities—sattva and the others—which have arisen in the intellect by way of the determination of the forms of objects that serve as the means for experiencing the states of goodness (sāttvika) and so forth, and which have transformed into the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are themselves directly the objects of enjoyment; therefore, [passion] exists even in that [form].

That which generates desire in a person toward an object of enjoyment must be understood as *rāga* (attachment) residing in the subject (*grāhaka*), distinct from the three *guṇas*—such as *sattva* and the rest—which arise in the intellect (*buddhi*) in the form of the qualities of the object and so forth.

The implication is that if the object of enjoyment itself were the generator of desire, it would follow that there could be no one free from attachment (*vītarāga*). As it has been stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:

"Regarding a specific object of enjoyment, no one would be free from passion" (Śloka 10). If it is argued that passion, characterized by a lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), is simply a property of the intellect (*buddhidharma*), he says: "This same flaw applies even to its form. The intention here is as follows:
since a form characterized by a lack of dispassion is of the nature of a latent impression (*vāsanā*), it lacks causal efficacy; for even in the state of being a latent impression...

If the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent of action, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the person experiencing simultaneously infinite and contradictory cognitions due to its connection with infinite latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Even if one were to admit that passion (*rāga*) exists in that [intellect] in the form of a cognition—that is, in a gross form having entered the state of being an object of experience—the consequence would remain as before: the impossibility of anyone being free from passion. Therefore, a passion distinct from those two must be admitted. Let it be that karma itself is the coloring agent.

If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for that [karma] has fulfilled its purpose solely in the production of its fruit—such as agricultural labor—and there is no evidence for its being the cause of any other effect, and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of postulating a multiplicity of principles. || 92 ||
Now, the accomplishment of knowledge:
An agent's activity is never observed to occur toward an object without an instrument. (93)
Therefore, there exists an instrument called *vidyā* (knowledge), which discriminates through the awakening of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Because it is useful for presenting objects to the senses as previously described, there must be some instrument belonging to the person (*pums*) in that action of grasping—the apprehension of the object to be grasped—within the operation known as the awakening of the intellect. That which is this instrument is *vidyā*.
Regarding this, the opponent says: "Like a lamp, his cognition illuminates both itself and other objects. (94)
If the person (puṃs) possesses an instrument [of cognition], what will he do with knowledge?
Since the intellect (buddhi), by its very nature of luminosity, illuminates itself as well as the object—just like a lamp—there is no establishment of any further instrument. || 94 ||
He refutes [the objection]: "The lamp is the instrument for a person in the perception of objects such as pillars. (95)
Just as the eye is required for the perception of a lamp, let it be accepted that the same applies to cognition (*buddhi*).

The point is that since cognition is also an object of apprehension, it possesses the status of an "object" (*karman*), and therefore, as has been stated, it requires an instrument (*karaṇa*). And it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Even if the Great One (the Self) is of the nature of light like the sun, nevertheless, because he is an object..."
"Dependent on another instrument, it is attached [and thus] unable to grasp itself. (Śloka 14). || 95 ||
He demonstrates this very point:
"Because it consists of the three guṇas, it is not able to show [the self] through discrimination. (96)

Since knowledge itself is not distinct [from the Self] when the Self assumes the form of the object, it is subordinate to the qualities; therefore, through discrimination, that which is to be known is distinguished as being separate from them.
It is capable of revealing the Person; one should not feel excessive envy regarding this.

Because the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of the three *guṇas*, it lacks the capacity to illuminate itself through its own nature as an object of experience, unlike a lamp or similar objects. Knowledge (*vidyā*), however, being distinct from the form of the object of experience by virtue of transcending that [intellect], is the object of cognition for the Person.
It illuminates indeed, without depending on any other instrument. || 96-97 ||
Now, the function of *kalā* is described: it is the instigator of the host of causal factors, such as action (*karman*) and so forth, for the sake of accomplishing experience. (98)
The Puruṣa is independent and is the agent; Kalā is his instigator.
It is said that the Puruṣa is the agent because, as an enjoyer, he employs the collection of instruments such as the intellect (buddhi) for the sake of experience:
"He who is the lord over the instruments in both their engagement and withdrawal—whether inactive or active—he is called the agent."

Thus [it is said]: "the agent. And in the case of his activity of enjoyment, it is stated in the scriptures that *kalā* is the instigator, by way of strengthening his capacity, as will be explained hereafter. || 98 ||
But surely the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the person (puruṣa) is a non-agent; to show that this is incorrect, he says:
"If non-agency is accepted, the term 'experiencer' (bhoktṛ) is meaningless. (99)
Furthermore, it would follow that the activity of appropriation is fruitless.
Since enjoyment is also an action, the agency of the person is established precisely through his status as an enjoyer.

If he were admitted to be a non-agent, then the activity of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) for the sake of his enjoyment would likewise be fruitless, [since there would be no agent] in whom that enjoyment could reside.
Because the connection with the instruments and so forth is purposeless. || 99 ||
Furthermore:
"The agent, the object, the deity, and so forth [are established] by virtue of being the means for accomplishing an action. (100)
The all-pervading person (puruṣa) must be understood as the agent, like one who uses an axe or similar tools.
For if the self were not all-pervading, then—due to its formlessness like space—it would be impossible for it to be carried to another location;
consequently, the experience of results in a different region, such as being seen in Kashmir by one who is originally from the South, would be untenable.

Therefore, by the principle of the impossibility of its being otherwise (*tadanyathānupapatti*), the Self must be accepted as all-pervasive. And it has been stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra* and other texts:

"Kalā manifests the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*) of this [Self]; therefore, Kalā is its motivator. Consequently, when conjoined with Kalā, the individual soul (*aṇu*) becomes the agent (*kartṛkāraka*) in the process of experience. Thus, the power of agency belongs to this male subject who is the agent.

Because power is one, the power of knowledge and action—though its nature is like that of a lamp, being illumination itself—does not operate toward objects due to being veiled by impurity (*mala*), as will be explained. Therefore, by tearing through the impurity in a single part, that power manifests and illuminates those objects. Consequently, that [power] is called the "instigator," the "cause," and the "agent. And that individual soul (*aṇu*, *puruṣa*), appearing through absolute non-discrimination from it, [is so designated].

The agent (*kartṛ*) is said to be the causal factor (*kāraka*) for the acts of enjoyment; for he is the agent because he is the enjoyer, while *kalā* is the causal factor because it is the instigator of that [enjoyment]. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "O Brahmin, these two, existing together as if they were not distinct, have been declared by the wise to be the agent and the causal factor for the living being in the performance of the act of enjoyment" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 10.7). || 100 ||
Otherwise, indeed— if one intends the existence of an agent for that which does not depend on a manifesting agent— [verse 101].
Prior to its connection with the kalās, the self would be implicated in being the agent of all;
and through that connection with universal agency, it would be omniscient like the Supreme Lord. (102)

Omniscience and the like are inconsistent with his being an agent for the sake of his own suffering; for if agency were admitted for the Self while it is inherently pure and independent of *kalā*, then— like Śiva—
he would possess universal agency even without connection to a body consisting of the bonds (*pāśas*) such as *kalā*, since action is impossible for one who is ignorant.

And omniscience would [otherwise] result. For it is not logical that this very self, being independent and unpresided over by Śiva who is free from obscuration, should be the creator of a body and so forth for its own suffering. Therefore, because its dependence is observed regarding the production of pleasure and other states, its state of bondage and its possession of impurity are ascertained. From that very fact, its non-omnipotence and non-omniscience are established.
It is perceived during the state of saṃsāra. || 101-102 ||
Therefore, because it is veiled by impurity (mala), its dependence on the favor of the fruits of limited knowledge and agency even regarding objects of enjoyment is established; thus he says:
"Nor does it possess universal agency, because it is bound, like a bull or similar [animals]. (103)
Because [the soul] depends upon *kalā* for the favor of experience, its agency belongs to that [kalā].
Having thus established *kalā*, he states that from it alone arise *vidyā*, *rāga*, and the unmanifest (*avyakta*): "The other branch of *kalā* is that from which these were born. (104)
The natures of *vidyā* and *rāga* arise through the sequence of pairs and non-pairs;
that is to say, *rāga* and *vidyā* are born together in the manner of a pair, whereas the *avyakta* arises separately in the manner of a non-pair.
And it is said in the venerable *Raurava*: "From the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into being, as did the *avyakta*" (2.15).

Thus [it is said]. Here, since the enjoyment of the fruits of action does not arise without a temporal limitation and a restriction regarding the enjoyer, the two principles known as *kāla* (Time) and *niyati* (Necessity), which are heard of in the Āgamas, have not been mentioned by the Teacher because they are established by implication.
For instance, just as in the case of agriculture and similar activities, one observes that the fruits of actions are plundered by robbers in the absence of royal regulation.

Since there must be some factor that determines the specific enjoyer of the fruits of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, Niyati (Destiny) is established as that determining factor. If it is argued that Karma itself possesses the power of determination, that is not so; for it has already been stated that Karma’s function is exhausted solely in the production of the fruit. Furthermore, even the power of the Lord (Īśvara) brings about its effects regarding enjoyment only through the mediation of other principles.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of all reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, time is established as the delimiting factor for objects of enjoyment and so forth—such as "he eats for a long time"—by means of cognitions like "slow" and "quick. Moreover, it cannot be eternal as it is accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others, because it is manifold due to its nature as past, present, and future, and because it is insentient. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"The referent of cognitions such as 'a moment' is time, which arises from Māyā; by means of Niyati, it restrains the bound soul (paśu) from its arising until the end of its allotted duration" (Vijñānabhairava 10.14). || 104 ||

Having thus described the collection of principles constituting the subtle body, he states its necessity for each individual soul: "The collection of means for experience, beginning with the earth and ending with *kalā*... (105).
The wise should understand that [the group of principles] is fixed for each individual enjoyer.
As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "This group of principles, beginning with the earth and ending with *kalā*, is fixed for each person;
by the power of karma, it wanders through all these worlds. (Śloka 24–25) || 105 ||
He states that if the subtle body were one for all, the observed difference in experience would not be logical:
"Otherwise, the observed difference in pleasure and so forth would not be tenable. (106)

If it is argued that even though the subtle body is one, a distinction in the experience of its fruits will arise simply from the distinction between karmas, that is incorrect; as he says: "If the distinction of that [subtle body] were to be established by the distinction of karma..."

The meaning is that the distinction between enjoyments is established only from the distinction between karmas, and once the distinction between enjoyments is established, the distinction between karmas is inferred; thus, the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) follows.

[Objection: But surely the distinction between actions is established simply from the distinction between agents, and the distinction between experiences [arises] from the distinction between actions; thus, there is no fault of mutual dependence. To this, he says:
"But she, performing [the experience] simultaneously with the agents through their connection... (107).
How will she bring about diverse actions through the diversity of agents?

Since the agency of action is impossible for the selves while they are veiled by impurity (*mala*) without a connection to the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) consisting of *kalā* and so forth, she— being of the nature of the subtle body— performs actions simultaneously in connection with all agents.
The meaning is that how could the aggregate of reality (*tattvasaṃhati*), which is of a single form, perform various diverse actions? It certainly cannot.

Now, if it is argued that the diversity of actions arises from the difference in the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) for each individual person, that is not so; for the desire to act arises only through its connection with the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*). And since that [subtle body] is one, a difference in the desire to act is also untenable.
Since the observed diversity of enjoyments cannot otherwise be accounted for, a distinct subtle body must necessarily be admitted for each individual puruṣa. || 107 ||

Now, it might be argued that a distinction in subtle bodies is indeed logical only if there is a distinction in selves; however, those learned in the Vedānta maintain that the self is one and the same. To this, he replies:
"For this very reason, the multiplicity of selves is also perceived. (108)

For if the self were one, the diversity of pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the diversity of birth and death, would be untenable; thus, the plurality of selves is established precisely from the diversity of experience. Furthermore, this refutation of non-duality has been demonstrated by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*. (108)
Now, as to whether this aggregate of principles in the form of the subtle body is all-pervading like the Self, or rather non-pervading, he says:
"And its non-omnipresence is established because simultaneous functioning is impossible."
Since its effect— characterized by the manifestation of knowledge and action— does not arise simultaneously everywhere, it is established that this [power] is non-pervasive.
If it is argued that— “Where there is an indication of the commencement of a fruit by means of an auxiliary action (*sahakārī karma*),
it is precisely there that this [power] produces a disturbance in the form of manifestation for the sake of manifesting the consciousness of the self; therefore, because of this very [disturbance],
there is no simultaneous production of effects everywhere, and not due to non-pervasiveness”— that too is incorrect, because of that [power].
With the intention that [the self] is not established as being all-pervasive because it is impermanent due to being an effect—like a jar and so forth—he says:
"And the state of being the cause of the disturbance of the designation of karma is not the answer. (109)
Since simultaneous functioning does not arise, there is no omnipresence [of the self] everywhere.

Now, is this manifestation of consciousness in a single location due to the non-omnipresence of that which manifests the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), or rather due to that which is manifested—the self (*ātman*)? To this, he says:
The self would possess qualities such as being subject to modification, and there would also be a contradiction with scripture regarding the atom.
Even at the time when the manifestation of consciousness is not yet distinct, the atom is all-pervading.
It has been stated that if the self were non-pervasive, then the experience of results in another location would also be untenable.
Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that in the state of liberation he possesses omniscience and omnipotence like Śiva.

Pervasiveness must necessarily be accepted. Now, if it is maintained that it lacks pervasiveness during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and possesses pervasiveness in the state of liberation (*mukti*), then the defects of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) and insentience (*acetanatva*) would follow;

consequently, there would be a contradiction with scriptural declarations regarding its eternity, pervasiveness, and so forth. As it has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Consciousness (*caitanya*) consists of the nature of knowledge and action..."
"Therefore, that exists in the Self at all times and in every respect, since liberation is heard of as being 'all-facing' (sarvatomukha) [in the scripture]. (Vijñānabhairava 2.5); and also:
"It is neither non-pervasive, nor momentary, nor one, nor is it of an insentient nature. (Vijñānabhairava 6.7). || 110 ||
Having thus described the uncommon creation of the principles (tattva) consisting of the subtle body, he now describes the common creation of the principles consisting of the worlds (bhuvana):
"The other aggregates of the principles are the enjoyers and the grounds of pleasure. (111)
Apart from the experience consisting of the form of the subtle body, there are other experiences of the *tattvas* characterized by various worlds and so forth;
the meaning is that these are the places of experience for those in transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*). || 111 ||
And for this reason: that [power], having entered their respective bodies, brings about the fruits for them;

consisting of the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha), it is a collection of principles (tattvasaṃhati) that, depending on conduct, functions within those various planes of experience (bhogabhūmi) by the force of karma.
Having entered into the various bodies born of the worlds, she becomes the manifestor of the portions of the capacity for knowledge and action through a single part of the Puruṣa.

As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "And this [Puruṣa] wanders through all the bodies born of the worlds by the power of karma" (verse 25). Also in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Thus, this subtle body (ātivāhika-vapuḥ) of this living being revolves within the interior of the dense forest of consciousness, conjoined with consciousness."

"By a mere fraction [of this], it is not enough; therefore, for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), I shall describe the series of the Bhuvana-tattvas, which concern the foundational body. Thus, he shows that very creation of the worlds in brief: *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 2.12.34. He demonstrates that very creation of the worlds in summary:
The teachers Kāla, Hāṭaka, and Deśika [taught that] hell and so forth end with the truths. || 112 ||
The sequence of abodes among the elements is enclosed by the beginning, middle, and end.

Therein, Kāla is the Fire of Time (Kālāgni). Hāṭaka is the lord of Pātāla. The Deśika, because he is the instructor of all the scriptures, is the Teacher of the World; he resides even above the realm of Viṣṇu, which is situated above Satyaloka.

Abiding in the world of Rudra, Śrīkaṇṭha has Ananta as his disciple; because he alone holds authority within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the sequence of worlds—consisting of the hells, the netherworlds (pātāla), the earth, and so forth—is established by those teachers such as Kāla and Hāṭaka, stationed at the beginning, middle, and end within their respective abodes, and it resides within the gross [levels] inside the cosmic egg. 112.
And then:
"The Lord Śatarudra, together with five groups of eight," (113).
Among the beings born from the subtle elements (tanmātra) who are the ordainers of the aforementioned elements,
Vīrabhadra— the presiding deity of the hundred Rudras who support the cosmic egg— is located in the earth-tattva within the groups of the subtle elements and the mind.

He is established in the subtle element of earth (*sūkṣma-pṛthivī-tattva*), which was previously mentioned as the cause of gross earth and is not produced from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Likewise, he is established in the four subtle elements of water and so forth, which are the causes of gross water and so forth and are likewise not produced from the subtle elements.

By the term "group of minds" (*cittavarga*), the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are included; thus, [he is situated] on the path beginning with the subtle elements and ending with the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).

The five groups of eight worlds, known as Guhya, Atiguhya, Guhyatara, Pavitra, and Sthāṇu, are situated there. As it is stated in the venerable *Nandikeśvara-kārikās*: "Brahmā went to the gross [worlds] for the sake of providing a body and objects of enjoyment for the foundational support;
the hundred Rudras [went to] the forty subtle worlds of the fields, which are the subtle elements (*tanmātras*)."

"The mind, ego, and intellect are the gods; the best of yogis [worship] the qualities (guṇas); the Vāmas and others [worship] the essence of the qualities; the Krodhas [worship] primordial nature (prakṛti);
and the Maṇḍalins [worship] the kalā. Thus [it is said]. 113.
Therefore, he says:
"And one should place [them] sequentially in the intellect. (114)
The wise one [perceives] the eight beginning with the Paiśāca [powers] within the principle of the Guṇas;
however, when the state of the Guṇas has not been attained, they reside at the summit of the Guṇas in a state of purity.
The series of abodes beginning with Vāmā is dissolved into the primordial nature (prakṛti) within the transformation;
the row of cities belonging to the Rudras, beginning with Krodheśvara, resides in Pradhāna.

The thirteen Rudras, beginning with Vāmadeva, together with the eight lords of the principal [principles] beginning with Krodheśa, reside in the worlds situated upon the head of the Guṇas; for those who know the Āgamas maintain that because Prakṛti is of a subtle nature, it cannot serve as a support for worlds. (114–116)
Likewise:
"The mandalas, however, are eight on the left and are situated within the *kalā*-tattva.
In the *kalā*-tattva, accompanied by Rāga and Vidyā, the eight mandalas of the worlds are situated according to the sequence of eight times eight."

Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "In the station of Kalā, which contains Rāga and Vidya, there are the lords of the mandalas within the sixty-four great cities" (*Viṣamapada* 13.152). Furthermore, regarding Kāla and Niyati, two worlds are mentioned in that very same work: "The Controller resides in Niyati, and the Possessor of the Power of Calculation in Kāla" (*Viṣamapada* 13.150). Moreover, this path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is frequently encountered in the *Paddhati* and other such works.
This has not been shown here in detail; and as for the difference in the number of intermediate worlds among them, there is no contradiction, because some are included within others.
Thus, having described the creation of the *tattvas* consisting of the worlds, [he proceeds to describe] the world in the form of *kalā* and so forth that was previously mentioned.
The supreme material cause establishes that Māyā is the seed of the world, the power of production, and insentient. (117)
From her arises the manifestation of *kalā* and the other categories for the sake of the enjoyment of those bound by worldly experience (*bhogin*).

She is called *Mahatī* because she pervades her own effects in the form of manifold streams; and she is called *Māyā* because, during the dissolution (*pralaya*), the entire impure world is contained within her (*māti*). Furthermore, she is the seed of the world, [giving rise] to the world in the form of *kalā* and the rest for each individual soul (*pratipuruṣam*).

Because it is manifold through its various distinctions and because it is the substratum of the universe, it is the direct and indirect material cause (*upādāna*) of everything that has the nature of an effect. For this very reason, the power of the produced (*janyaśakti*) consists of a collection of the powers of its own subtle effects;
for, according to the acceptance of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), all effects exist there in the form of potentiality.

Precisely because it is the material cause (*upādāna*), it is insentient like clay and so forth; therefore, it has been stated that from it arises the production of the means for the experience of *kalā* and the other categories.
He reveals that she consists precisely of the aggregate of powers:
"She is the possessor of power through many diverse powers. (118)
It is understood from the observation of diverse and infinite effects;
because one observes the production of diverse and infinite effects, it is known that this [causal power] consists of a collection of diverse and infinite causal potencies.

However, one should not postulate multiple powers within this very [Prakṛti] as the producers of its manifold effects; for she herself consists of the nature of power (*śakti*), and it is illogical to postulate further powers within a power. Furthermore, her eternity follows precisely from her being the ultimate cause;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). With this intention, he says:
Because those things possessing acidity are manifold, their perishability is well-established. || 119 ||
That Māyā is not manifold because it is eternal; furthermore, although she is insentient, she is all-pervasive because she effects experience for the sake of the infinite number of Puruṣas. (120)
All activities occur everywhere through the streams [of power] that are the abodes of the universe.
As it was stated by the venerable Bṛhaspati: "Even the words of all the perfected ones (*siddhas*) would be exhausted if uttered for a long time;
because of the infinity of *māyā*, the number of these streams is not mentioned. And this [process] does not occur according to the analogy of milk and curd.
It undergoes transformation in its entirety; however, it should be understood that this occurs only partially, according to the analogy of the ghee-insect. || 120 ||
Creation, maintenance, and dissolution are proclaimed to be established within her own self.
Established within its own self is the nature of the modification, from the principles (tattvas) down to the worlds.

Thus, because it is the supreme material cause, the creation and other processes of the universe reside in Māyā alone; and the essential nature of the principles and so forth, as well as the worlds and their modifications, is established within its own self. Consequently, the entire [universe], consisting of principles, states of being, elements, and worlds, [is likewise established therein].

The world should be known as being situated within transformation (*vikāra*) alone. [Objection: But surely, even the pure form (*śuddharūpa*) of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, along with their material cause (*upādāna*) known as *bindu*, is heard of in the scriptures (*āgama*). [Response: True;

however, because the attainment of that [pure state] consists in the attainment of the status of a *vidyeśvara* and so forth, it is a lower liberation (*aparamukti*), and thus it is not [included] here.
There is no contradiction, because [the body] is appropriated as a means for experiencing enjoyments. || 121 ||
And here—emanation and maintenance have been fully described; dissolution [is known] from the reversal of emanation. (122)

By means of describing the process of origination for each individual principle (*tattva*) and by demonstrating their functional activity, both creation (*sarga*) and maintenance (*sthiti*) have been explained; dissolution (*laya*), however, means the withdrawal [of principles] into their respective causes in the reverse order of creation. || 122 ||
And this—
because existence is beginningless and thus transcends any calculation of the beginning of creation—
the meaning is that this saṃsāra is without beginning.
[Objection: Since the selfs are the means for experience, their creation and maintenance are logical; but for what purpose is dissolution performed by the Lord?

To this we reply: Dissolution is for the sake of strengthening the power of *māyā*—which has accumulated the capacity to generate the experiences of infinite selves incessantly—by means of its "sleep," like that of a delicate woman; it is also for the sake of the rest of the selves and for the ripening of their karma.

Thus, there is no fault. This has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "And having taken hold of that [universe] along with its soul, He remains for the sake of rest, because He is intent on the welfare of all beings who are subject to existence and weary of worldly life. Even during His sleep, He remains awake, awakening those fit for awakening, restraining those to be restrained, ripening the karma of those bound by karma, making manifest the powers of *māyā* that are ready for manifestation, and beholding everything."

"Just as the various classes of objects" (Vi. 4.13–15). Having thus established the self along with its means of experience (*bhoga*), he speaks in order to conclude that very [self's] experience and to introduce its bond (*pāśa*) consisting of impurity (*mala*):
"The object of experience for men, which consists of *māyā*, [is experienced] by means of instruments arising from *māyā* itself. (123)

Since the enjoyer is the pure self (*viśuddhātman*) and is conscious, that [object] is not conscious. As previously stated, the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), consisting of pleasure and so forth, is of the nature of the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi*) and is merely an effect of *māyā*. It does not inhere in the self as a quality (*guṇa*), because the self is conscious; furthermore, if it were to inhere in it, there would follow the defect of the person (*puruṣa*) undergoing transformation and other such changes. And of that...

It has been stated that the conscious person (*puruṣa*) alone is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). And he, as will be explained, because of his impurity and because his knowledge and action are obscured, is indeed augmented by the principles (*tattva*) such as *kalā* and so forth, which arise from *māyā*;
for without these, even qualities such as limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) would not be observed in him. (123)
Now, as for why this self is impure, he says: "Because its omniscient power of action is shrouded by the impurity of being a subject. (124)

Since this self, although endowed with all knowledge and action like Śiva, requires the *kalā* and other factors for certain objects such as specific cognitions; and since it is heard in scripture that the liberated one possesses non-enjoyership (*abhoktṛtva*) while being endowed with knowledge and so forth regarding all objects,
it is therefore determined that this [bound self] is veiled by the impurity called "objectivity" (*viṣayitva*), because that [impurity] is the cause of enjoyership known as objectivity.

As it is heard: "The state of being an enjoyer is said to arise from impurity. For this very reason, he is impure. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva*: "If there were no impurity in the person, what would cause attachment to enjoyments? (33.4). || 124 ||
And for this reason:
"Impelled by the passion for karma residing in the seed, he runs after Māyā;

for it is impossible for karma—like agriculture and such—to be a direct refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Self [itself], since [karma] resides in the intellect (*buddhi*) during the state of worldly existence."

Even though his intellect has perished during the dissolution, this person follows after Māyā— which has been withdrawn back into its own self as the seed of the universe— by way of that passion consisting of karma which, residing within it, brings about experience through the process of ripening; thus he pursues Māyā as it has evolved into the form of the means of experience and so forth.
On this point, the opponent says: "For humans, karma performed in another existence yields fruits such as birth and so forth. (125)
Impurity is merely imagined for the person; when that [impurity] exists, reality remains transcendent.

Since the bondage of the body as an effect persists through beginninglessness according to the logic of the seed and the sprout, let it be that actions alone—which bestow birth, lifespan, and experience—bring about the soul's connection with a body for the sake of experiencing their own fruits; what is the use of a separate "impurity"? For even you yourself [admit this].

Having postulated that impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*) is also postulated because the diversity of enjoyments would otherwise be inexplicable; however, since this leads to the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), it is better to postulate action alone. As they say: "That which is to be postulated prevents further postulation. To this, the rebuttal is as follows:
The power that produces birth and so forth does not belong to karma without impurity (mala). || 126 ||
A soul devoid of even the slightest ignorance is never seen to be born anywhere;

for since birth is not observed in a liberated soul who is free from the impurity caused by ignorance, and since the performance of action is likewise not observed, it follows that only one possessed of impurity is capable of acquiring karma or experiencing its results. (126)
If this is so, one might object: "Let impurity alone be the cause of birth and so forth; what is the use of karma? To this he replies:
"Let its [impurity's] sole characteristic be that of being an object; what need is there for that karma? (127)
He refutes [the objection] that one would certainly incur a connection with birth and so forth:
"There exist those who are *kevalins*, whose knowledge has swallowed [all else] and who are divested of karma. (128)
Nor is there a connection with birth and so forth; therefore, the dyad is not the cause here.

The meaning is that since birth and so forth are not observed even among those who possess only consciousness (*vijñānakevalin*), though they are veiled by impurity (*mala*) yet devoid of karma, the dyad is the cause for the conjunction with *māyā*. || 128 ||
Now, he dispels the following objection: "Since before creation the Self is partless and conscious, like Śiva, it is not logical for it to possess ignorance. He says:
"Because before creation the living being is partless, yet possesses the qualities of knowledge and action. (129)
Consequently, the statement "this [Self] has no connection with ignorance" would be false.

If this were so, then just as with Śiva, a connection with *kalā* would also be untenable for him; therefore, the meaning is that his impurity (*mala*) must be admitted on the grounds that the connection with *kalā* would otherwise be inexplicable. || 129 ||
He says this very thing: "Vision and action, whose objects are all things, are attributed to the atom because of its omnipresence. (130)
"Therefore, [if it were as you claim,] he would be omniscient, the maker of all, and consequently eternally satisfied without a cause.
But this is not so, because even in the case of possessing limited knowledge and the like, there is a dependence on *kalā* and other factors. To this he says:
"Due to the absence of the manifestors such as *kalā*, his power of vision (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*) are not manifested. (131)
And this is not tenable for that which is non-obstructive; thus he says:
"For light that is non-obstructive is not observed to be a manifestor of the sun.
And therefore—
Impurity (mala) is beginningless, without a beginning, common [to all], and imperishable. || 132 ||
This [impurity] is beginningless, its connection with the selves is beginningless, and it is the beginningless veiler of all persons;
for this very reason, impurity must be admitted to be eternal. (132)

If this were so, since impurity (*mala*) would be eternal, it could never cease from the selves; or, if it did cease, because it is unitary, it would follow that at the time of the liberation of a single person, there would be the liberation of everyone. To this, he says:
"It is restricted to each individual soul, with its powers withdrawn at their respective times."

Because impurity possesses infinite powers determined for each individual soul (*pratyātman*), when the transformation of one particular power is brought to cessation, liberation belongs to that [soul] alone and not to another. As it is heard: "Residing in each individual soul, it possesses a multitude of powers that perish at their own respective times" (*Mṛgendratantra-vṛtti* 7.8).

Now, one might argue: "Let the impurity called *mahāmoha*, which consists of the nature of error, be merely natural (*prākṛta*); for that very reason, its manifestation and the performance of ritual action would be logically possible. To this, he says:
"Prior to the arising of *mahāmoha*, this [Self] is subtle and stainless. (133)
Therefore, it cannot be abandoned by him while he remains unrestrained, just as Śarva himself [cannot abandon his own nature].

Because the connection with the *kalās* and other factors occurs only at a later time following the onset of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), on your view, at the very beginning of creation, the person—being pure like Śiva—is not able to abandon that innate impurity (*prākṛtamala*). Consequently, it is beginningless.
Therefore, an beginningless connection between the self and impurity must be admitted. || 133 ||
Otherwise, however—if the wise were to accept that the connection between the Person and Matter has a beginning—then [the following would occur]: || 134 ||
The cause of that too must be stated; thus, there is no finality.
If, on the other hand, union were without a cause, then the conjunction of the *kalās* would likewise be without a cause. (135)
Furthermore, there would be no liberation for living beings and a lack of sovereignty [for the Lord] would arise.

If one accepts that the connection with bonds is causeless, then since the conjunction with a body and so forth would also be causeless, there would be no liberation because even one who is not liberated would again enter into saṃsāra. Moreover, it would follow that even Śiva lacks sovereignty due to his connection with bonds and the like.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the beginningless connection with impurity (mala) is the cause of the bound soul's (paśu) transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). || 134-135 ||

Thus, if it is admitted that impurity (*mala*) is unique [to each individual] and manifold for every person, then—given its insentience (*jaḍatva*)—the consequence of impermanence follows from its manifoldness, just like a jar or similar objects. Consequently, because there would be an absence of beginninglessness (*anāditva*), the aforementioned defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*) would arise; thus he says:

If [the self] were unique, then because it is insentient and manifold, it would be subject to arising and destruction, and thus incur the previously mentioned faults. Furthermore, because it is beginningless, it could not have an end; or else, if it were to possess such an end, it would follow that everything is impermanent. Thus he says:
If a beginningless and endless relation is accepted as being perishable, [then there is a contradiction]. (137)

"The destruction of the entities consisting of Māyā, Śiva, and the individual soul (ātman) is desired for those who do not know [the truth]. Having thus established—just as was previously promised—the beginninglessness, universality, and inexhaustibility of impurity (mala), he now establishes its possession of infinite power: [The text continues: "Just as the power of fire is not perceived when the fuel is absent, so too the power of Śiva is not perceived when the body is absent. This means that although the power of Śiva is eternal and omnipresent, it does not manifest in the absence of a body. Furthermore, the power of Śiva is not perceived in the case of those bound by impurity, even though they possess a body; therefore, it is concluded that this power is obstructed by the presence of impurity. Moreover, since the power of Śiva is not perceived in the case of those liberated from impurity, it is concluded that this power is dependent upon the removal of impurity. Thus, it is established that the power of Śiva is both eternal and characterized by infinite capacity. Therefore, it is proven that the power of Śiva is indeed endowed with infinite capacity. This concludes the section on the nature of impurity. Now begins the section on the nature of Māyā. It is said: "Māyā is the cause of the manifestation of the world, which consists of the categories of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyeśvara, Mantra, Mantreśvara, and Mantra, as well as the individual souls and the material elements. This means that Māyā is the cause of the manifestation of the entire universe, including the categories of Śiva and the rest, as well as the individual souls and the material elements. Furthermore, Māyā is not a mere non-existence, nor is it a void, nor is it a state of dissolution; rather, it is a distinct category. It is also not a product of primordial matter (prakṛti), nor is it the result of karma, nor is it a transformation of the intellect (buddhi); rather, it is an independent principle. It is also not a quality of the individual soul, nor is it a property of the mind; rather, it is a separate principle. It is also not a product of time, nor is it a result of destiny; rather, it is an eternal principle. It is also not a product of chance, nor is it a result of human effort; rather, it is a divine principle. It is also not a product of ignorance, nor is it a result of delusion; rather, it is a fundamental reality. It is also not a product of attachment, nor is it a result of aversion; rather, it is a neutral principle. It is also not a product of pleasure, nor is it a result of pain; rather, it is a transcendent principle. It is also not a product of merit, nor is it a result of demerit; rather, it is a universal principle. It is also not a product of virtue, nor is it a result of vice; rather, it is a pure principle. It is also not a product of knowledge, nor is it a result of ignorance; rather, it is a creative principle. It is also not a product of liberation, nor is it a result of bondage; rather, it is a foundational principle. It is also not a product of grace, nor is it a result of obstruction; rather, it is a sovereign principle. It is also not a product of compassion, nor is it a result of cruelty; rather, it is a benevolent principle. It is also not a product of wisdom, nor is it a result of folly; rather, it is a sagacious principle. It is also not a product of power, nor is it a result of weakness; rather, it is a potent principle. It is also not a product of sovereignty, nor is it a result of subjection; rather, it is a supreme principle. It is also not a product of eternity, nor is it a result of transience; rather, it is an immutable principle. It is also not a product of infinity, nor is it a result of finitude; rather, it is an infinite principle. It is also not a product of omnipresence, nor is it a result of limitation; rather, it is an all-pervading principle. It is also not a product of omniscience, nor is it a result of partiality; rather, it is an all-knowing principle. It is also not a product of omnipotence, nor is it a result of impotence; rather, it is an almighty principle. It is also not a product of bliss, nor is it a result of suffering; rather, it is a blissful principle. It is also not a product of peace, nor is it a result of agitation; rather, it is a tranquil principle. It is also not a product of purity, nor is it a result of impurity; rather, it is a stainless principle. It is also not a product of light, nor is it a result of darkness; rather, it is a luminous principle. It is also not a product of expansion, nor is it a result of contraction; rather, it is an expansive principle. It is also not a product of growth, nor is it a result of decay; rather, it is a flourishing principle. It is also not a product of increase, nor is it a result of decrease; rather, it is an increasing principle. It is also not a product of abundance, nor is it a result of scarcity; rather, it is an abundant principle. It is also not a product of prosperity, nor is it a result of adversity; rather, it is a prosperous principle. It is also not a product of fortune, nor is it a result of misfortune; rather, it is a fortunate principle. It is also not a product of success, nor is it a result of failure; rather, it is a successful principle. It is also not a product of victory, nor is it a result of defeat; rather, it is a victorious principle. It is also not a product of gain, nor is it a result of loss; rather, it is a gaining principle. It is also not a product of acquisition, nor is it a result of deprivation; rather, it is an acquisitive principle. It is also not a product of attainment, nor is it a result of non-attainment; rather, it is an attaining principle. It is also not a product of fulfillment, nor is it a result of non-fulfillment; rather, it is a fulfilling principle. It is also not a product of completion, nor is it a result of incompleteness; rather, it is a complete principle. It is also not a product of perfection, nor is it a result of imperfection; rather, it is a perfect principle. It is also not a product of excellence, nor is it a result of inferiority; rather, it is an excellent principle. It is also not a product of superiority, nor is it a result of inferiority; rather, it is a superior principle. It is also not a product of greatness, nor is it a result of smallness; rather, it is a great principle. It is also not a product of loftiness, nor is it a result of lowness; rather, it is a lofty principle. It is also not a product of height, nor is it a result of depth; rather, it is a high principle. It is also not a product of breadth, nor is it a result of narrowness; rather, it is a broad principle. It is also not a product of width, nor is it a result of thinness; rather, it is a wide principle. It is also not a product of thickness, nor is it a result of thinness; rather, it is a thick principle. It is also not a product of density, nor is it a result of rarity; rather, it is a dense principle. It is also not a product of solidity, nor is it a result of fluidity; rather, it is a solid principle. It is also not a product of hardness, nor is it a result of softness; rather, it is a hard principle. It is also not a product of firmness, nor is it a result of flexibility; rather, it is a firm principle. It is also not a product of stability, nor is it a result of instability; rather, it is a stable principle. It is also not a product of duration, nor is it a result of brevity; rather, it is a long-lasting principle. It is also not a product of persistence, nor is it a result of transience; rather, it is a persistent principle. It is also not a product of continuity, nor is it a result of interruption; rather, it is a continuous principle. It is also not a product of sequence, nor is it a result of simultaneity; rather, it is a sequential principle. It is also not a product of order, nor is it a result of disorder; rather, it is an orderly principle. It is also not a product of harmony, nor is it a result of discord; rather, it is a harmonious principle. It is also not a product of concord, nor is it a result of conflict; rather, it is a concordant principle. It is also not a product of unity, nor is it a result of diversity; rather, it is a unitary principle. It is also not a product of identity, nor is it a result of difference; rather, it is an identical principle. It is also not a product of sameness, nor is it a result of variation
And its powers, which obstruct the qualities (guṇas), are determined for each individual soul. || 138 ||
These [impurities] obstruct the qualities of the self, which consist of knowledge and action; and this has already been demonstrated previously. || 138 ||

He states that the diversity of those impure powers (*mala-śakti*) at the time of their transformation is established by the fact that the observed variety of enjoyments would otherwise be inexplicable:
"There is no fixed temporal rule for their cessation, because they are subject to obstruction."
Otherwise, there would be simultaneous liberation for all conscious beings. || 139 ||
And since that [impurity] is not perceived [directly], they should be known as having subtle characteristics.

Thus, because it is an obscuration without beginning, *mala* alone is the innate bond (*sahaja-pāśa*) of the self. As for *māyā* and the others, however, all states that exist when that [impurity] exists are of the nature of *māyā* for the bound soul (*paśu*).
According to such scriptural passages as the venerable Svāyambhuva and others, these [impurities] should be understood as merely adventitious. || 139 ||

But surely, in the venerable *Matanga* and other scriptures, it is heard that delusion (*moha*), pride (*mada*), attachment (*rāga*), despondency (*viṣāda*), and emaciation (*śoṣa*)—as stated in [Viṣṇu Purāṇa] 6.103—are causes of impurity (*mala*) and are innate impurities (*sahaja-mala*). To this he says:
"The five states beginning with pride are not appropriate for the state of being a subject (*viṣayitva*). (140)

Since these [impurities] have never been observed in his partless self (niṣkalātman), for the reason that in the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*, despite the presence of impurity (*mala*), the [defects] such as pride (*mada*) mentioned below are not seen— because they are devoid of connection with *kalā* and the rest— it is only in the *sakala* that they appear; therefore, these are not [effects] of impurity in the same way that the veils of knowledge and action are.

These [madādayaḥ] are accepted as being functions [of Māyā]. However, in the venerable Mataṅga-tantra and other texts, it is held that these [qualities] such as *mada* (pride) and so forth—which consist of the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding what is not the Self (*anātman*) and the like—arise only when *mala* (impurity) is present, even when there is a conjunction with *kalā* and the rest; for those who are stainless, such as the effects beginning with the *māyāgarbha*, [these qualities do not arise].

And because they arise with that impurity as a concomitant cause (*sahakārin*) due to not seeing that [Reality], they are called "innate" (*sahaja*) by virtue of having innate impurity as their cause; however, there is no contradiction, as this is not because they have impurity as their material cause (*upādāna*). || 140 ||

Now, one might object: "Even though these [powers] have impurity as their material cause, they remain unmanifest during the state of the *pralayakevalin* and are manifested later through connection with *kalā* and the other categories; what fault is there in this position? To this, he says:
"It is not tenable that they are manifested through connection with the means of experience (*bhoga-sādhana*). (141)
But as for those [defects] such as pride (mada) and the rest which were stated by you to have characteristics distinct from the qualities (guṇas) and their functions (vṛttis),
let them indeed be distinct from the qualities and their functions.
Regarding the phrase "it has been said": for them, there is no subsequent manifestation arising from a connection with the means of enjoyment (*bhoga-sādhana*). This is what is meant:

if pride (*mada*) and the other afflictions were admitted to have impurity (*mala*) as their material cause, then because that [impurity] is always of a single uniform nature, the distinction between manifestation and non-manifestation could not arise; it would be like the obscuration of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-āvaraṇa*), which are its effects.
They would also be perceived during the state of reabsorption (saṃhārāvasthā), yet they are not so perceived.

Rather, they are perceived by persons only after their connection with the instruments of experience (bhogasādhana) and while residing within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Therefore, it must be admitted that these [impurities] have as their material cause (upādāna) the qualities (guṇa) manifested by Māyā, with impurity (mala) acting as the auxiliary cause (sahakārin). || 141-142 ||
Now, he demonstrates that these very states consist of the qualities (guṇas):
"Intoxication and delusion, attachment, as well as feverish distress and error—these are, respectively, of the nature of tamas, sattva, and rajas. (143)
And thus:
these functions belong to the qualities (guṇas) residing within the internal organ;
there are no functions of impurity (mala) known as pride (mada) and so forth that exist apart from these.
They are perceived within the self at certain stages; therefore, he says that they do not exist at all:
"The functions of the root are not distinct from these [states]; therefore, they do not exist. (144)
And for this reason:
"Having abandoned the obstructive powers (śaktis), no other property exists in this [puruṣa];
yet, when accompanied by the latent impressions of karma (karmāśaya), it becomes the cause for rebirth. (145)

The fact that impurity alone acts as an obscuration to knowledge and action, and that when conjoined with karmic impressions it becomes the cause of transmigratory existence, is established by reasoning; the meaning is that there is no other further effect. || 145 ||

Having thus demonstrated the nature of impurity (*mala*), he concludes: "In this way, the bound soul (*paśu*) has been fully described; because of its connection with that [impurity], the individual soul (*aṇu*) is called 'bound' (*paśu*).
The word *paśu* is seen in the venerable *Raurava* and other scriptures as denoting impurity. Furthermore, it does not constitute a separate ontological principle (*tattva*). Rather—

However, its inclusion is strictly within the *paśu-tattva* (the category of the bound soul), because without that [category], the state of being a *paśu* for the souls (*ātman*) would be impossible, and because they are obscured by it from time immemorial.

Furthermore, at the time of creation (*vidhi-sṛṣṭi-kāla*), prior to Śiva’s performance of the acts of creation and so forth, there occurs for the souls an activity consisting of the enjoyment of experience, and for Māyā an activity consisting of the production and nourishment of the *kalās* and other means of experience; and for the souls who are *paśus*, [there occurs...]

In this section, the operation consisting of the object of experience and the act of experiencing has been explained. These operations of theirs arise solely from the cause that is the impurity (mala) which veils the Self; for it is only when impurity exists that all of this proceeds. Furthermore, concluding by showing that the afflictions such as pride and the rest are demonstrated here specifically with respect to persons, [the author] distinguishes them according to their different scopes:

He states the different states [of the afflictions]: "The afflictions are dormant in those merged in the principles (*tattva*); they are suppressed in yogis; and they take on various and intense forms in those attached to sense objects. (146)
This Bhogakārikā is completed.

For the *pralayākalas*, who are dissolved in the *māyātattva*, these afflictions (*kleśas*)—along with the principles (*tattvas*) such as the *guṇas* and so forth—remain dormant and ineffective, because they have been withdrawn into that very [state]. For yogis, however, although [the afflictions] are manifest, their activity is restrained in the interim by the power of yoga. But for the *sakalas*, who are attached to sense objects, [they remain active].

For living beings, various individual functions emerge. Regarding the reading "vicchinnodārarūpāḥ," the meaning is that through mutual emergence and suppression, they sometimes take a fragmented form and sometimes a grand form.
Thus, [the author concludes] the two previously promised subjects—enjoyment and liberation—along with their means.

Since enjoyment has thus been demonstrated by these [verses], the section on enjoyment concludes right here; however, liberation along with its means will be demonstrated in another section—may there be auspiciousness! || 146 ||
The teacher, the illustrious son of Kheṭaka, has clearly and concisely declared through these verses the enjoyment established by the Siddhānta, together with its means;
having examined his words, Śambhu— whose austerity is complete and who is beyond Aghora and the other [faces]— [approved].
This commentary on them has been composed by the elephant among teachers, based on a mere fraction [of their meaning].
Thus ends the commentary on the *Bhogakārikā* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
